studies.explainEasier: If you hold your ground and stay careful, they may still rush at you. Your Lord will then send even more help. Five thousand angels with clear marks on them will come down to your side.

studies.title: Only Good News For You
studies.meaning: God says plainly what the angels were for, and it was not military. He made it good news for you, and He made it so your hearts would settle. Then the point lands with no hedging on it: help comes only from God. Early scholars read this as heading off a natural mistake, because a promise of thousands of angels invites the thought that the numbers are what does the work. The verse says the numbers were for the hearts. The outcome was never a matter of counting.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, closing the passage about angels inside the account of the battle. Early scholars treat this verse as the key to the two before it, since it says what the promise was actually for. The surah's bigger argument about that day is being set up right here. The community's confidence had to rest somewhere other than on an advantage they could see.

keyTerms.note: From the root behind announcing glad tidings, and behind the change that comes over a face at good news. It names the message, not the thing announced, which is the very line this verse draws.
From a root describing ground that is level and still, and a heart at rest. It pictures reassurance as settling rather than as excitement, a quieter image than the English suggests.
From the root for coming to someone's aid, the same one used of the disciples earlier in this surah. It names help given, so victory is something received rather than achieved.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Morale was treated as a real weapon in Arabian warfare. Commanders spread word of allies coming, of fresh men on the road, of losses on the other side. A force that believed it was backed fought differently from one that did not. Everyone knew that what men believed about their numbers counted for as much as the numbers themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: The line saying victory comes only from God appears twice in the Quran, here and in Surah 8. Both times it sits inside an account of a battle. Both times it lands right after a mention of angels sent as reinforcement. That repetition, in settings so closely matched, is one of the tightest parallels between the two surahs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God separates what did the work from what was given to steady you. Thousands of angels are described as sent for the sake of the hearts, and never as the thing that decided the day. That keeps unseen help from being counted up like a resource. It guards against two mistakes at once: leaning on visible strength, and leaning on invisible strength as though it were the same sort of thing.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing in nearly identical words, after the reinforcement at Badr.
Says later in this surah that if God helps you, nobody at all can overcome you.
Names what hearts actually settle by, which is the remembrance of God.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between what actually does the work and what was given to steady you. Most reassurance is the second kind, and mistaking it for the first is how people end up let down by things that were never holding anything up. Ask which of your current supports is which, and be honest about one of them.
studies.explainEasier: God sent that news to make you glad and to settle your hearts. The angels were not what won the day for you. Help only ever comes from God, who is strong and wise.

studies.title: None Of It Is Yours To Decide
studies.meaning: Two purposes are named for what happens in a battle, and they are offered as alternatives. One is to cut off a portion of those who refuse. The other is to push them down so they go home with nothing at all. Then the address turns personal and draws a line. None of this is yours, whether God turns to them in mercy or punishes them. Early scholars report the occasion behind it. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), wounded and grieving, had started naming particular opponents in prayer against them.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside the account of the battle at Uhud. The community had taken heavy losses, including close relatives of many who were standing there. Early scholars report that the Prophet began naming opponents in prayer and that this verse came down after it. Several of the men named are reported to have joined the community later on. The sources say that bears directly on how the verse should be read.

keyTerms.note: The word for the far end of a thing, a limb or a border. Cutting off an edge describes something reduced rather than destroyed, which is what the alternative here offers.
A verb for humbling someone by frustrating him, tied to grief and to turning back thwarted. It names the defeat of an intention rather than the defeat of a fighting force.
A participle from the root for a venture that failed, used of a hunt that comes home with nothing. It names the state of someone whose whole effort returned him nothing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Cursing an enemy by name was a recognised practice. A man wronged in battle was expected to call down harm on the people who had wronged him. Poets composed such calls formally, and whole communities repeated them for years afterwards. Then, in the middle of a day of losses, word came that the matter was not his at all. That cut straight across what grief in that culture was permitted to do.
studies.didYouKnow: The limit here lands in the middle of a sentence. The line about mercy or punishment breaks into a description of what God does in a battle. Early scholars point out that the interruption is itself the point. The instruction arrives inside the account of the very day that provoked it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God takes the final verdict away from the one man with the best claim to want it. Someone wounded and bereaved is told that what happens to his opponents is not his business, and that holds both ways, mercy or punishment. His grief keeps every ounce of its weight and is given no authority at all. What later became of some of those men suggests why the door was kept open.

crossReferences.why: Follows straight on, stating that God forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.
Tells the Prophet his job is to deliver the message, and the reckoning belongs to God.
Repeats the same limit: you are a reminder, and not someone set in charge of them.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone who has genuinely wronged you, and notice how much of your inner argument is about what should happen to them. This passage does not ask you to forgive them or to stop hurting. It takes the verdict out of your hands, which is a different thing, and often more of a relief than forgiving would be.
studies.explainEasier: God may cut down part of the enemy force, or push them back so they go home with nothing. Either way, it is not up to you. God decides whether to forgive them or punish them.

studies.title: Forgives Whom He Wills
studies.meaning: The limit set in the verse before is now given its reason, and the reason is ownership. Everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, so what becomes of any of it is His to settle. Then two clauses arrive in perfect balance: He forgives whom He wills, He punishes whom He wills. The verse does not leave them level, though. It closes on two names taken from the vocabulary of mercy, and early scholars read that as tilting the sentence without cancelling either half.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. It comes directly after the verse saying that the fate of the Prophet's opponents is not his to decide. Early scholars read the two together as one argument: a limit is placed on a man, and then the reason for it is given. The verse belongs to the account of the battle at Uhud. Its content is general, though, and the tradition quotes it entirely on its own.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to cover, the same one behind the Arabic word for a helmet. Forgiveness is pictured as covering a thing over rather than rubbing it out, unlike the English.
A strong form of the same root, naming not one act but a settled and repeated habit. Where it sits, at the very end, is what gives the whole sentence its direction.
The second of the two closing names, from the root shared with the word for a womb. Paired with the first, it joins the covering of faults to a compassion that keeps going.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ownership settled everything in Arabian life. A man could do as he liked with his own camels, his own well and his own land, and nobody asked him about it. Claims and disputes were nearly always arguments about who owned a thing, not about who might use it. So a statement about God's freedom, resting on ownership, spoke in the plainest terms those listeners had.
studies.didYouKnow: The two names that close this verse appear together more than seventy times in the Quran, which is more often than any other pair of God's names. They nearly always come at the end of a verse rather than at its start. They are there to close a passage, not to open one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God states two outcomes in exactly the same shape, and then breaks the match with the names at the end. That is done on purpose. Nothing is promised to anyone here, and yet the sentence refuses to stop halfway. Resting it all on ownership matters too. It means mercy and punishment come out of one fact about God, and not out of two moods pulling against each other.

crossReferences.why: Sets the limit this verse explains, that the outcome is not the Prophet's to decide.
Answers a claim to special standing with the same statement of ownership and will.
States the widest form of the mercy that this verse's closing names point toward.

studies.applyIt: Read the two halves of this verse aloud and notice they are the same length and shape, then notice where the sentence actually ends. That ending is a choice the text is making. The next time you find yourself running through what somebody deserves, put the closing words where the text puts them and stop there.
studies.explainEasier: Everything in the sky and on the earth belongs to God. He can forgive anyone He chooses, and He can punish anyone He chooses. The verse ends by calling Him the One who forgives again and again.

studies.title: Doubled And Doubled Again
studies.meaning: This is addressed to believers, and what it names is lending at an increase that piles up: a debt doubled, then doubled again on top of the doubling. Early scholars describe the exact arrangement meant here. A debtor who could not pay on time had the sum raised and the deadline pushed back. A small loan could grow past any hope of ever being repaid. Then the two verses after it set the instruction inside something much larger, tying being mindful of God, and obeying, to the hope of mercy.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, and these lines sit inside the account of the battle at Uhud. Early scholars treat that placing as chosen rather than accidental. A community that has just been through loss and division is addressed about how its members handle each other's money. The practice named was ordinary in Arabian trade. This surah touches it only briefly, since a far longer treatment comes in an earlier surah.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to grow or swell, used of a hill rising out of a plain. The word names the increase itself, not the lending, which is why the Quran describes it by what it does.
A noun paired with a participle from its own root, so the phrase doubles the idea of doubling. The sound of it performs the very compounding that the sense describes.
From a root meaning to split open, used of a farmer breaking the earth. Success in Arabic is cutting through to what lies underneath, rather than piling things on top.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Credit ran everything in Mecca and Medina, and there was no court anywhere to restructure a debt. A man who could not pay on the day went to whoever held the loan, and the usual terms were more time in exchange for a bigger sum. Families lost their land that way, and sometimes their freedom. Everyone had watched a neighbour disappear into exactly that sequence.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah handles the whole subject in three short verses, tucked inside a passage about a battle, while a far longer treatment sits near the end of Surah 2. Early scholars discuss how the two relate to each other. Part of what they weigh is the placing here, among verses about loss and division inside the community.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God sets this instruction between two verses that widen it a long way. One warns about guarding yourself from the Fire. The other ties obeying to the hope of mercy. That frame treats money as part of the same life as everything else, not as a department of its own. And the setting inside a hard battle adds something more. How a community handles its own members bears on how it stands when it faces outward.

crossReferences.why: Treats the same subject at length, including the order to give a struggling debtor time.
Contrasts what is lent to grow among people's wealth with what is given seeking God's face.
Describes a loan given to God instead, and multiplied many times over.

studies.applyIt: This passage puts money inside a chapter about loss, division and mercy, which suggests they belong together. Take one money arrangement you are part of, and ask what it does to the relationship around it. Not whether it is allowed. Just what it does to the two people standing inside it.
studies.explainEasier: Do not lend money and keep piling more and more onto what someone owes you. Be careful of God instead, and stay away from the Fire. Do what God and the Messenger say, and you may be shown mercy.

studies.title: The Race And Its Runners
studies.meaning: God tells you to run, and then describes the people who arrive, and it is not a list of heroics. Giving when money is easy and when it is not. Swallowing anger while it is still hot in your chest. Pardoning people who are plainly in the wrong. Early scholars notice the order: holding the anger in comes before pardoning, because containing it is the step that makes forgiving possible at all. And the first thing named at the finish is forgiveness, not the Garden.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. This sits in the long section working through the defeat at Uhud and everything that came after it. The verses just before warn against piling interest onto a debt. The ones just after describe people who sin, remember God, and do not keep at it. So the passage belongs to a stretch about a community handling its own failures, in money and in war, and not to a description of untested piety.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of filling a waterskin to the brim and tying it shut. The anger is not gone. It is held in, and the strain of holding it is part of what the word carries.
Not displeasure but the heat itself, the anger felt before a word is said or a thing is done. Naming it apart from the response shows the feeling is not what is being criticised.
A form of the verb that carries competing with others, not just moving fast. The picture is a field of runners, which is why what is raced toward is pardon and a garden, not a chore.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In tribal Arabia an insult left unanswered was a debt. Honour worked like credit: a slight had to be repaid, usually with interest, and a man who let one go could find his household treated as fair game. Feuds ran for generations over a wounded camel or a line of verse. So praising the man who absorbs an offence and gives nothing back turned the whole social sum upside down.
studies.didYouKnow: The width of the Garden is given in almost these same words in one other place, at 57:21, where the phrase uses the singular heaven instead of the plural used here. Both passages open with a command to race. And in both of them the width comes before any description of what is actually inside.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God measures you by what you do with your own temper and your own money, in good times and bad, which puts the test inside ordinary Tuesday life rather than in some rare moment. Then the closing line shifts the frame again. These qualities are not set out as entry requirements so much as a description of people God loves. That makes the Garden sound less like a wage and more like where such people belong.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same picture of racing toward forgiveness and a garden that wide, in a Medinan surah.
Names forgiving while still angry as a mark of those who answer their Lord.
Carries the list on into those who sin, seek forgiveness, and do not knowingly keep at it.

studies.applyIt: The next time anger rises at home, try holding it for the length of one slow breath before you answer. You are not pretending it is not there. You are testing whether the sentence you were about to say is the one you actually want to have said. Notice what changes in that gap.
studies.explainEasier: Hurry towards God's forgiveness and a garden as wide as the sky and the earth. It is for people who give when things are good and when they are hard. They hold their anger in and forgive others.

studies.title: They Remember And Ask
studies.meaning: These are people who fail, and then do one particular thing. They have done something indecent, or wronged themselves. And they remember God and ask Him to forgive them. Then a question breaks into the sentence and answers itself: who forgives sins but God. What comes at the end carries real weight for the early scholars. They do not keep at what they did, and they know what they are doing. Failure is simply assumed here. What gets described is the shape of the recovery, not how to avoid the fall.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, inside the passage describing people who are mindful of God. It comes straight after the call to race toward forgiveness. Early scholars note where it falls, inside the surah's account of a battle in which the community had genuinely failed. They read it as spoken to men who were, at that very moment, going back over their own conduct.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to go past proper bounds, used of anything gross or beyond measure. It names a serious wrong, and sits here beside the milder phrase about wronging oneself.
The same verb the Quran uses throughout for remembering God. Putting it first, as the response to a wrong, makes recollection the hinge, before any resolve about the future forms.
From a root suggesting tying tight, and a sound that will not stop. It names holding on stubbornly, so what is ruled out is continuing, not slipping again after a lapse.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a small town there was nowhere private in which to fail. A wrong was known, talked about, and remembered for years. The usual answer was to defend yourself, because admitting a fault cost your family its standing along with your own. So owning up, instead of explaining yourself, cut against every social pressure that world had.
studies.didYouKnow: The question in the middle of this verse, asking who forgives sins but God, cuts into a description of people in order to say something about God. The Quran breaks in like this in other places too. Early scholars note that the sentence then picks up again as if nothing had interrupted it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God builds the portrait of a mindful person around failure, not around a clean record. What marks these people out is an order of steps: remember, ask, and do not dig in. And the words about knowing are demanding. They rule out keeping at a wrong and then blaming it on not having realised. What is being asked for is honest recognition of the fault.

crossReferences.why: Describes these same people just before, racing toward forgiveness and holding their anger.
Says whoever does evil or wrongs himself and then seeks forgiveness will find God forgiving.
Addresses those who have gone furthest, telling them not to despair of God's mercy.

studies.applyIt: The order here is worth copying: remember, ask, stop. Most people run it backwards. They resolve to stop first and never get round to the remembering. The next time you catch yourself in something, name God before you promise anything about the future. Then see whether the promise comes out any different.
studies.explainEasier: When these people do something wrong, they think of God and ask Him to forgive them. Nobody else can forgive sins. And once they know a thing is wrong, they do not keep on doing it.

studies.title: The Reward Of The Workers
studies.meaning: The reward arrives in two parts, and the first one is a surprise: forgiveness from their Lord, named before any garden is mentioned. Early scholars notice that order, because a list of rewards that opens with pardon is assuming there was something to pardon. Then comes the familiar picture of gardens with rivers running under them, and a closing line praising the reward of those who work. That last word counts. They are called workers, not the righteous and not the believers, which ties the reward to effort.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. This closes the description of the mindful that began with the call to race toward forgiveness. Early scholars place the whole passage inside the surah's handling of the battle at Uhud. The community had just failed, and here it is described in words that begin with pardon. That setting is what shapes how the sources read the order of the two halves.

keyTerms.note: From the root meaning to cover, so forgiveness is something laid over a fault rather than something that rubs it out. Naming it first makes the fault part of what the passage assumes.
A verb of praise used only in exclamations, with no plain statement sense at all. Arabic keeps it for commendation, so the clause it opens is pure approval and nothing else.
The participle from the ordinary verb for doing and working. It names people by their labour rather than by their belief, which is a striking choice at the close of this description.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A worker was paid at the end of a job, and the whole relationship came down to that moment. Harvest work, caravan work and building were all settled on completion. People talked about a generous employer for years afterwards. The line of praise that closes this verse is the kind of thing said about a man who paid more than anyone expected. The first listeners heard it in that key.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about gardens with rivers running beneath them appears more than thirty times in the Quran, and this surah alone holds several of them. The chapters they sit in were revealed years apart, and what surrounds the phrase shifts a little each time. It is one of the most familiar patterns in the whole text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting forgiveness at the top of a list of rewards tells you who the reward is for. These are not people who never failed. They are people who handled failing in a certain way, so pardon is what they need first and it is named first. Calling them workers at the end keeps effort in the picture. It also stops effort from becoming the whole basis of what they are given.

crossReferences.why: Describes the people this reward is promised to, and what they do after a wrong.
Uses the same exclamation about the reward of those who work, at the end of a scene.
Describes the same gardens in more detail, with rivers of different kinds beneath them.

studies.applyIt: Notice that the first item on this list is being forgiven, not being rewarded. If you have been holding yourself to a standard where mistakes rule you out, the order here is worth sitting with. Read the verse before this one and this one together, in that order, and see what they treat as perfectly normal.
studies.explainEasier: These are the people God forgives. He gives them gardens with rivers running under them, and they stay there for good. The verse ends by saying how fine a reward that is for people who work.

studies.title: Patterns That Have Run Before
studies.meaning: The word translated ways means settled patterns, worn in by repetition. So the instruction is to go out and look at where those patterns ended. History is offered as evidence here, not as comfort. Then the address turns inward, and two things are forbidden: going slack, and grieving, in that order. The promise of coming out on top is tied to faith, and not to numbers. Early scholars read that condition as the whole point of the passage.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. This part of the surah speaks to the community after the reverse at Uhud, in the third year after the migration. Some seventy Muslims were killed there, and the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was wounded in the fighting. Early scholars read these verses as spoken into that particular grief. A defeat had happened, and the real question was what to conclude from it.

keyTerms.note: A path worn in by being walked. The plural names regular patterns in how communities rise and fall, treating history as something with a grain rather than a string of accidents.
From a root for feebleness and slackening, used of a rope losing its tension or a bone going frail. What is forbidden is not feeling weak but letting the slackness settle in.
Counsel meant to soften a person rather than to inform him. It names speech that works on the will, which is why the same sentence sets it apart from guidance and plain statement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The instruction to travel and look was practical advice, not a figure of speech. Meccan caravans ran north to Syria past the abandoned rock-cut dwellings at al-Hijr, and south to Yemen past ruined dams and dead towns. Traders knew these places as landmarks, camped near them, and told stories about them at night. A merchant hearing this could name the sites he had already walked through.
studies.didYouKnow: Three different words for the same revelation turn up inside one short verse: a clear statement for all people, guidance, and counsel for those mindful of God. The group being spoken to narrows across the three, and early scholars notice that. What reaches everyone as news becomes guidance, and then counsel, only for those who bring something to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God offers history as evidence anybody can go and check, which puts part of the case for revelation outside the book itself. Then the comfort that follows is remarkable for what it does not say. It never promises the loss will be reversed or explained. It hangs the promise of coming out on top on a condition instead. So the reassurance stays honest about where the community actually stood that week.

crossReferences.why: Carries straight on, explaining the defeat as days turned between people rather than abandonment.
Repeats the instruction to travel and inspect what became of stronger civilisations.
Pairs the same two words, going slack and being uppermost, in a later Medinan surah.

studies.applyIt: Think of one setback from this year that you have quietly filed away as proof you are not up to something. Write down what actually happened, in two sentences, with no conclusion attached to it. Then notice how much of your discouragement came from the event and how much came from the verdict you added.
studies.explainEasier: Other peoples lived before you and their stories ended. Travel and look at what happened to them. Do not go weak and do not be sad. If you truly believe, you will come out on top.

studies.title: Days We Turn Between People
studies.meaning: The comfort here does not soothe; it compares. A wound reached you, and a wound like it reached them. Then comes a rule, carried by a verb used of passing a thing from hand to hand around a circle. Days are turned about among people, and nobody holds them for good. Two reasons are given for that turning. One is about what becomes known, the other about who is taken. Early scholars stress that the knowing is not God learning anything. It is a state being brought out where it can be seen.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in the surah's account of the battle at Uhud. The community had won at Badr and lost here. Early scholars read the comparison as aimed at the particular shock of a setback that follows a victory, which is harder to take than a plain defeat. The passage answers it by making the turning of such days the ordinary state of things.

keyTerms.note: A word for an open wound, from a root also tied to hardship and to something breaking the skin. It names the injury rather than the defeat, which keeps the comparison physical.
From a root meaning to pass a thing round in turns, which later gave Arabic its word for a state. It pictures days circulating among people rather than being awarded to anyone.
The same word this surah uses for those who testify. Its double sense joins the one who bears witness to the one who dies doing it, and the Arabic holds both at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fortune in the peninsula plainly went round in circles. A tribe on top in one generation was cut down in the next by drought, a lost caravan or a defeat. The same families rose again ten years later. Nobody expected it to hold, and the family histories carried the memory of both. So the picture of days passed round like a bowl at a gathering needed no explaining.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb here for turning days about among people comes from the root that later gave Arabic its everyday word for a state or a government. The link is no accident, since both name something that changes hands. Early Arabic dictionary writers treat that turning as the basic sense the whole root is built on.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God puts a defeat inside a pattern without explaining it away. Such days turn about, so the setback is not favour being withdrawn from you. What the turning does, He says, is show something. What could not be told apart before now becomes plain. That makes hardship a time when things come clear rather than a time of correction, and it is a very different account of why it happens.

crossReferences.why: Names the second purpose at once: to refine those who believe and wear away refusal.
Asks whether you thought you would enter the garden without what came to those before you.
Says the same thing plainly: We will test you until the strivers and the steadfast are known.

studies.applyIt: Notice how this verse opens. It does not say your wound is small. It says the other side is wounded too, which is a particular kind of comfort and works better than most. The next time something hurts you, ask honestly what it cost the other party. The answer is very rarely nothing.
studies.explainEasier: If you have been hurt, the other side has been hurt too. Days like this are turned round between people, and nobody keeps the good ones for ever. God is letting it show who really trusts Him.

studies.title: You Wished For This
studies.meaning: Three short verses press hard, one after another. The first names what hard days do: they refine one group and wear the other away. The second asks whether you expected the garden before God had picked out those who strive and those who hold fast. The third cuts deepest. You used to wish for death before you met it, and now you have seen it with your own eyes. Early scholars tie that last line to the men who had urged going out to meet the attacking force.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in the account of the battle at Uhud. The classical sources say that going out to meet the attacking force was pressed by younger men who had missed the earlier battle and wanted the same chance at it. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) would rather have stayed inside the city. The sources agree that the majority view carried the day.

keyTerms.note: A verb used of purifying gold and of getting out whatever was mixed in. It describes a process that takes away rather than adds, which is why it suits an account of a costly day.
From a root used of the waning moon losing its light. It names a slow rubbing out rather than sudden destruction, and it is paired here with the verb for refining metal.
A verb for wishing and for picturing something you want. It names desire aimed at what is not in front of you, which is exactly what the verse then sets against having seen it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Young men in Arabia grew up on poetry about courage and on the names of relatives who had fought. Missing a famous battle was a shame that followed you around for life. So the wish to be tested was real, and it formed early. What that wish actually meant was learned once, in a single afternoon, and the men who learned it were often barely grown.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs in the first of these verses come from completely different worlds. One is used of refining metal in a fire. The other is used of the moon losing its light night by night. Set inside one short sentence, they put a cleaning process next to a shrinking one, and the roots alone carry the whole contrast.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God will not let entry into the garden be assumed. The sorting has to happen, He says, and He puts it in events rather than in anything people say about themselves. Then the third verse adds something harder to hear. Wishing for a thing and living through it are not the same, and the gap between them is not called a failure. That gap is what being tested means.

crossReferences.why: Asks the same question, whether you expected the garden without what came to those before.
Asks whether people thought they would be left alone for saying that they believe.
Describes what actually happened on the day this passage is looking back at.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have said you wished for that would be genuinely hard: more responsibility, a test of your patience, a chance to prove something. Sit for a moment with what it would actually involve on a Tuesday afternoon. This verse is not mocking the wish. It is asking you to know what you asked for.
studies.explainEasier: God will show who really believes and who does not. You cannot expect to walk into the garden before you are tested. Some of you wished for death before you met it. Now you have seen it close up.

studies.title: Only A Messenger
studies.meaning: A rumour ran across the battlefield that the Prophet had been killed, and the answer that came back is a statement about what a messenger is. Muhammad (peace be upon him) is a messenger, and messengers have passed away before him. Then the question: if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels. Early scholars notice that the verse never denies the grief. It separates the man from the message. And it names the other road exactly: turning round, not losing belief.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, tied to the battle at Uhud. A cry went up on that field that the Prophet had been killed, and part of the force gave way. The classical sources agree on the incident. They also report this verse being recited in public at his death some years later, when the community could barely take the news in, and they describe the effect it had on them.

keyTerms.note: A verb meaning to become empty or to pass by, used of times gone and places left. It describes earlier messengers as having gone on ahead, not as having failed at anything.
An idiom for reversing direction, built on the word for a heel. It pictures retreat as walking back the way you came, and the surah uses the phrase again a few verses later.
From the root for gratitude. Closing a verse about a leader's death with a promise to the thankful is unexpected, and early scholars read it as naming what holds when a support is taken away.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tribe often held together because of one man. When a chief fell, alliances came apart, followers scattered, and a whole confederation could be gone within a season. People simply expected that, and the force facing them at Uhud was counting on it. So the question this verse asks was not asked for effect. It described what usually happened.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical sources report this verse being read aloud at the very moment the Prophet died. They describe the people there hearing it as though for the first time. Almost no other reading of the Quran, outside the setting where it first came down, is reported as widely as that one is.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God puts the staying power of a message somewhere other than in the man who carried it, and that claim reaches a long way. He also uses the gentlest words available for giving up, since turning on your heels is about movement and not about belief. What is at stake is how people behave under shock. And the closing promise goes to the thankful rather than to the steady, which puts the whole thing in a different key.

crossReferences.why: States the same fact plainly: you will die, and they will die.
Follows at once, saying no soul dies except by God's leave at an appointed term.
Asks whether, if the Prophet dies, the people addressed imagine they will remain.

studies.applyIt: Consider what in your religious life leans on one particular person: a teacher, a friend who keeps you honest, someone who leads your community. Now picture that person gone. This is not morbid, since it is the question the verse asks outright. Name one practice you would want to keep, and start doing it without reference to them this week.
studies.explainEasier: Muhammad is only a messenger, and messengers came and died before him. Some people would turn back the way they came if he died. That would not hurt God at all. God pays back people who are thankful.

studies.title: Death At A Written Time
studies.meaning: Two claims are laid side by side here. Death happens by permission and at a term already written, so no amount of courage brings it forward and no amount of caution puts it off. Then the reward comes: whoever wants what this world pays is given some of it, and whoever wants what comes after is given from that. Then a third thing is added that does not follow the pattern of the other two. A reward for the grateful, named with no limit on it.
studies.historicalContext: Medina. This comes out of the review of the battle of Uhud, in the third year after the migration. During the fighting a cry went up that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had been killed, and part of the army broke. These verses speak straight into that moment. Early scholars read the opening line as answering the very fear that made men run.

keyTerms.note: The word traders used for a debt with a fixed due date. Applied to a lifespan it makes death an appointment already written in a ledger, not an event waiting for a cause.
From a root meaning to come back. A reward is pictured as something returning to whoever sent it out, which is why one word covers both the worldly and the lasting kind.
A participle, naming a settled leaning rather than an act. It closes a verse about wanting, which suggests the third option is not another want but a different hold on whatever arrives.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debt in Medina and Mecca was written down with a named term, and the whole trading world turned on those dates. A caravan financed in spring against repayment when it came home. A marriage payment put off. A settlement falling due at the next harvest. Everyone knew the difference between money owed now and money owed on a date. This verse borrows that vocabulary for the length of a life.
studies.didYouKnow: The same split between two wants turns up at 42:20, except there it is put as farming rather than trade. The two aims are called harvests, and the man who wants the lasting harvest has his increased. Reading them together shows the Quran making one point twice, in the vocabulary of whichever audience it is speaking to.
studies.theologicalSignificance: By fixing the hour of death, God takes risk out of the calculation entirely. If the moment is already set, caution buys you nothing and courage costs you nothing. What is left to decide is only what you were aiming at, and it is the aim, not the outcome, that gets answered. Then gratitude is added as its own category. That suggests it is not one more thing to want, but a way of holding whatever comes.

crossReferences.why: States the same split between two aims, in the imagery of sowing and harvest.
Spells out what happens to the one who wants this fleeting life and the one who works for the next.
Repeats that God puts off no soul once its appointed term has come.

studies.applyIt: Take one decision you have been avoiding because of what it might cost you. Ask a narrower question than usual: what am I actually aiming at here. Say the answer out loud. Most hesitation dresses itself up as prudence, and this verse is interested in the aim underneath rather than in the risk on the surface.
studies.explainEasier: Nobody dies before the time God has set for them. If you want only what this world gives, you get some of it. If you want what comes after, you get some of that too.

studies.theme: The Love Between God and the Believer
studies.title: They Did Not Weaken
studies.meaning: The verse opens with how many, and then never gives you a number. Prophets before this one fought beside large companies of devoted people. Then three things are denied of those companies in a row. They did not lose heart at what struck them. They did not weaken. They did not give in. The verbs get more physical as they go. Early scholars discuss the rare word used for the men who fought alongside them, read either as great numbers or as the learned and devoted.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, in the account of the battle at Uhud and the days after it, when part of the force had given way. The passage answers that shock by setting the day inside a much longer history. Communities before this one met exactly the same thing and did not break. Early scholars read it as comfort and correction handed over together, with no individual named anywhere in it.

keyTerms.note: An expression for a large but unnamed number, stronger than the ordinary word for many. It leaves the count open, which is what makes the precedent feel long rather than particular.
A rare word early Arabic dictionary writers explain either as great numbers or as people devoted to the Lord. The Quran uses it only here, and the commentaries keep every reading.
From a root suggesting stillness and lowering yourself. It names the visible posture of surrender rather than the inward state, which is why it comes last of the three.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A beaten force in Arabia showed it by posture as much as by anything said. Men sat down, laid their weapons aside, and sent out someone to talk. Everyone knew the signs on sight. The three denials in this verse move from the inward to the visible, ending on the posture itself. The first listeners followed that as a description of the stages of giving up.
studies.didYouKnow: The rare word this verse uses for the men who fought beside the earlier prophets is found nowhere else in the entire Quran. Words that appear only once make up a known category in the classical scholarly writing. They draw long discussion for one simple reason. There is no second use anywhere to compare them against.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What God offers here is history rather than a promise. Nothing at all is said about how things will turn out. What is said is that other people stood where you are standing and held. Then it closes on God's love for those who endure, which ties the bond to the holding on and not to the result. So what that endurance is worth does not depend on how the day went.

crossReferences.why: Gives their words at once: a prayer for forgiveness, for firm footing and for help.
Describes a small band saying many a small group has beaten a large one by God's leave.
Closes the surah with the same vocabulary of endurance and of holding a position.

studies.applyIt: The three verbs here describe a sequence: losing heart, then weakening, then giving in. They are not the same thing, and the first can happen without the other two following. Notice which stage you are actually at with something difficult right now. Most people announce the third when they have only reached the first.
studies.explainEasier: Many prophets before this one fought with large groups of devoted people beside them. When hard things hit them, they did not lose heart, they did not grow weak, and they did not give up. God loves people who hold on like that.

studies.title: Their Only Words
studies.meaning: What those earlier companies said under real pressure is quoted here, and the wording insists this was all they said. The prayer has four parts and the order is a surprise. It opens with forgiveness, and not for wrongs done to other people but for their own going too far in their own affairs. Then it asks for firm feet, and only then for help. Early scholars notice that order. The request about their own conduct comes first, and the request for victory comes last. Most people under threat would say it the other way round.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, carrying on the description of earlier communities that met hardship and did not break. The passage sits inside the surah's account of Uhud. The classical sources report two things about that day: an argument over the command, and a rush to collect the spoils. Early scholars read this prayer's line about going too far in your own affairs straight against that background.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to exceed proper measure, used of spending and of any excess. It names overstepping rather than sin in general, so the confession is specific about the kind of failure.
A physical request, using the verb for fixing a thing in place and the word for feet. In a battle it means not being pushed back, and Arabic uses it for steady resolve as well.
From the root for coming to someone's aid, used all through this surah. Putting it last means the prayer asks for help only after asking to be repaired and then steadied.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A line of men held ground shoulder to shoulder, so the phrase about firm feet was no figure of speech to them. Sandals in loose ground, a slope, a stumble over a body: those things decided whether a line held or broke. Asking for steady feet was asking for the most solid thing a fighter could want. And it came before asking to win.
studies.didYouKnow: The prayer is quoted here in full, and the words in front of it say this was the whole of what they said. The Quran keeps a number of such prayers word for word. Several of them are in this surah, which holds more quoted prayers than most chapters of its length.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The order of the four requests is the whole argument. Asking first about their own excess treats the trouble inside them as the one to deal with first. Asking for firm feet before help treats endurance as what is really needed. Victory comes last, and briefly. So what you are like matters more here than how the day turns out, and God is asked in that order.

crossReferences.why: Records a nearly identical prayer for firm feet and for help, before an earlier battle.
Gives another prayer kept in this surah, asking that hearts not swerve after guidance.
Closes the surah with a longer prayer, which also begins by asking for forgiveness.

studies.applyIt: Look at the order of these four requests and set it beside your own prayers under pressure. Most of us start with the outcome and never get as far as our own conduct. Try reversing it once this week. Ask first about where you have overstepped, and let the request for help come last.
studies.explainEasier: This is all they said when things got hard. They asked God to forgive their sins and the times they went too far. They asked Him to hold their feet steady. Last of all, they asked Him to help them win.

studies.title: The Best Of Helpers
studies.meaning: One thread closes and another opens across these three verses. Those earlier communities were given the reward of this world and the better reward of the next, with a closing note about God loving those who do good. Then a warning to the believers, using the same picture of turning on your heels that came a few verses earlier. Then one short sentence that answers the whole thing: God is your protector, and He is the best of helpers.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, after the battle at Uhud, when advice about where the community stood and what it should do next was arriving from every direction. Early scholars tie the warning to that pressure. The short verse after it is read as the surah's answer, given with no argument attached. Its words for protection keep coming back through this whole section.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to come back, used of a garment returning to its owner. Reward in Arabic comes back to you rather than being paid across to you from outside.
From the same root as the word for a guardian used earlier in this surah. It covers protector, patron and the one who takes charge of your affairs, all inside one word.
A superlative built on the root for aid used over and over in this surah. The form implies there are other helpers, putting God at the head of a list rather than alone on it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: After a defeat, the real question in Arabia was whose protection you would go to next. Beaten groups made new ties quickly, because a party with no patron was finished. Advice arrived at once, and nearly always from somebody with a stake in the answer. The warning here belongs to that moment, when a community is at its weakest and easiest for someone else to move around.
studies.didYouKnow: The picture of turning on your heels comes up twice within a few verses of this surah. Once it is about the death of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). Here it is about taking bad advice. One image ties two very different dangers together, and the Quran uses the phrase in only a handful of places.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The answer to the warning is not a plan. It is a statement about who you belong to. Nothing is said about what to do next, and the community is simply told whose it is. That meets the real worry of that week, which was never about tactics but about who would stand behind them. And calling God the best of helpers, rather than the only one, leaves ordinary human help standing underneath.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same picture of turning on the heels, at the news of the Prophet's death.
Names God as protector with the same word, calling Him an excellent protector and helper.
Says shortly afterwards that if God helps you, then nobody can overcome you.

studies.applyIt: After a setback, advice arrives fast and most of it comes from someone with an interest. Think of a recent disappointment and list who offered you a view of it. Then ask, for each of them, what they wanted the situation to turn into. It is a clarifying exercise, and it takes about two minutes.
studies.explainEasier: God gave those earlier people good things in this life and better ones after it. Then believers are warned: follow people who reject God and you will be turned back and lose. God is your protector, and the best helper there is.

studies.title: Dread Cast Into Hearts
studies.meaning: What is promised here happens inside the other side rather than out on the field, and God names it as His own doing. Dread will be thrown into their hearts. Then a reason is given. They set up partners with God for which no warrant was ever sent down. Early scholars linger on that word warrant, because it says their claim has nothing to stand on, not merely that it is mistaken. The verse closes on their lodging, using a word for the place you settle into for shelter.
studies.historicalContext: Medina, after the battle at Uhud. The classical sources report that the attacking force pulled back without pressing its advantage on the city. People at the time found that hard to explain, given the state the community was in after that day. Early scholars link this verse to the withdrawal. The Quran itself states the rule rather than telling the story of any one event.

keyTerms.note: A word for fear that fills you and grips, marked off by early dictionary writers from ordinary fear by how suddenly it comes. It names an experience, not a judgement about danger.
From a root meaning power and dominance, used of an argument that forces agreement as well as of a ruler. Here it names the backing a claim would need to stand up at all.
From the verb to take refuge. Using a word for shelter of the fire is a deliberate reversal, since the place you run to for safety is named as the destination instead.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wars in the peninsula were often settled by nerve rather than by losses. A force that lost its confidence pulled back even while it was winning. Commanders knew that spirit could drain away overnight for no reason anybody could point to. This was plain experience and not superstition. It made what was going on inside an opponent a real thing to reckon with.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for dread appears only a handful of times in the Quran. In every one of them it is put into hearts, rather than rising up out of a situation. Early scholars note how steady that pattern stays across all the places the word turns up.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What God does here is inward and unseen, which fits the larger argument of this surah, that outcomes are not settled by anything you could count. And the dread is tied to a cause: a claim made with nothing at all behind it. So it is not arbitrary. What is described is a state that follows from standing on a false position, not a punishment dropped on someone from outside.

crossReferences.why: Uses nearly identical wording of the earlier battle, dread cast into the hearts of opponents.
Describes the same thing again, dread cast in from a direction nobody expected.
States earlier in this surah that help comes only from God, not from visible strength.

studies.applyIt: Notice that this verse describes something happening inside people, not to them. A position held with nothing behind it is uneasy to hold, whether or not anyone argues with you about it. If you are defending something you cannot really back up, that unease is telling you something. Name one such thing today, even if you keep it.
studies.explainEasier: God says He will put fear into the hearts of the people who fight against the believers. They set up other gods beside Him with nothing to back it up. Their home in the end is the Fire.

studies.title: Until You Faltered
studies.meaning: This is the hardest account of the day. God's promise had been kept, and the other force was being cut down by His leave. Then three things happened in order. You faltered. You argued over the command. You disobeyed, after being shown what you wanted. A split inside the community is then named without softening: some wanted this world, some wanted the next. And the passage ends where nothing in it had prepared for. He pardoned you.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and the classical sources agree on the incident behind it. Archers had been placed on high ground with orders to hold their position regardless of how the battle went. When the Meccan force gave way and plunder became visible, most left that position, the ground was retaken, and the day reversed. The Quran's account follows exactly that sequence.

keyTerms.note: A verb whose root covers both sensing and killing, used of harvesting and of striking down. Its use places the community's early success in unmistakably physical terms rather than abstract ones.
From a root meaning to pull in different directions. The form makes it mutual, so what is described is a group tearing at a decision rather than one party overruling another.
From a root meaning to wipe out a trace, used of wind erasing footprints in sand. Pardon in Arabic is the removal of the mark rather than the excusing of the act that made it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Plunder was how a raiding force got paid. Men who rode out expected a share, and taking it carried no shame. For many of them it was the point of the trip. That is what makes the failure at Uhud both ordinary and costly. The archers did what almost any force in Arabia would have done. The position they left was the one thing holding the field.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah names three failures in a row: faltering, arguing, and disobeying. Then it splits the community itself into those who wanted this world and those who wanted the next. Few passages in the Quran are as hard on the community they address. And it is kept in that community's own scripture.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage turns down every comfort on offer, then gives one nobody asked for. It does not soften the account. It does not play down the split. It does not blame the enemy's strength. Once the responsibility is fully set out, it ends on pardon, which comes as a gift rather than as a conclusion. Full honesty, then mercy: that is how this surah tends to move.

crossReferences.why: Continues the account, describing the flight and the sorrow that followed it.
Names the cause behind the turning away, and says again that God pardoned them.
Warns against disputing with one another, saying it makes resolve itself depart.

studies.applyIt: The order of this ayah is worth borrowing when you review something that went wrong. Name what actually happened, including your own part in it, in sequence and without adjustment. Then stop. Do not add the excuse or the explanation. The pardon in this passage arrives only once the account is finished.
studies.explainEasier: God kept His promise, and you were beating them. Then you lost your nerve, argued about the orders, and went against them once you saw what you wanted. Some of you wanted this world. Even so, God forgave you.

studies.title: Sorrow Upon Sorrow
studies.meaning: The scene is shown from behind. You were climbing away, not turning back for anyone, while the Messenger called from your rear. Then comes a strange clause. He paid you back with sorrow upon sorrow, so that you would not grieve over what you missed or over what struck you. The early scholars discuss which two sorrows are meant, and they set them out in more than one way. They read the purpose clause this way: a grief given to push out a smaller grief.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, carrying on the account of Uhud after the position was left. The classical sources describe how confused the retreat was. A rumour went round that the Prophet had been killed, and on that field it was hard to hear anything at all. They report the news that he was alive reaching men who were still scattered. The two sorrows are read against that order of events.

keyTerms.gloss: you were going up and away
keyTerms.note: A verb of ascending and of moving off into open ground. It describes the direction of the retreat physically, up the slope, rather than naming it outright as flight.
From the root for twisting, the same one used earlier in this surah of twisting the tongue. Here it means turning the head, so the denial describes running without a backward glance.
A word for grief that covers and constricts, from a root used of clouds covering over the sky. It names sorrow as something that presses down rather than as sadness merely felt.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A retreat up broken ground was chaos. Dust, noise and the slope made it impossible to see or hear more than a few paces, and men lost track of brothers and fathers within moments. Calls from behind were routinely inaudible. The detail that the Messenger was calling from the rear would have been heard as a fact about the field before it was heard as a reproach.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase read as sorrow upon sorrow is one word repeated with a small word between. Arabic uses that shape for layering, not for force. The early scholars disagree about which grief was which. That opening comes from the shape of the phrase itself, not from any gap in the reports.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A second grief is given so that a first will not be felt. That is an odd way to describe mercy. The larger sorrow was the fear that the Prophet had been killed, and it made the smaller ones stop counting: the lost plunder, the wounds. So a greater loss is treated as something that can reorder the small ones, not just add to them. The ayah presents that as meant.

crossReferences.why: Gives the sequence of failures that led to the flight described here.
Continues immediately with the security that came down over part of the force afterwards.
Describes another day when numbers failed and tranquillity was sent down afterwards.

studies.applyIt: Sometimes a large worry arrives and every small one goes quiet. Most people notice that and find it strange. This ayah presents it as intended. Think of a time it happened to you, and notice what the large thing revealed about the size of what it displaced. Keep that ranking when the small ones return.
studies.explainEasier: You ran up the hill and did not look back. The Messenger was calling you from behind. Then God gave you grief on top of grief. That way you would stop aching over what you lost that day.

studies.title: Sleep Sent Down As Security
studies.meaning: After the grief, something is sent down and it is described in two words: security, and then slumber. Sleep on a battlefield is the sign that fear has lifted. But it covers only part of the force. The rest are described as preoccupied with themselves, thinking of God in a way the ayah names as belonging to an earlier age, and asking whether any of the matter was theirs. The answer is given twice, and the passage closes on what hearts are being tested for.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the account of the aftermath of the battle at Uhud. The classical sources preserve reports from those present describing a drowsiness that came over them as they sat among the wounded, so heavy that weapons slipped from their hands. The same reports describe others awake through the night, running the day's decisions over. The ayah is read against both accounts.

keyTerms.note: From the root that gives Arabic its words for faith and for safety. It names the state rather than the sleep, so the slumber that follows is described as its symptom rather than its cause.
The specific word for the sleep that comes over a person before proper sleep. It names something that arrives rather than something taken, which is why the ayah can describe it as sent down.
A noun formed from the word for ignorance, used of the period before the message came. It names a way of thinking rather than a date, which is why a thought can be described by it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sleep after a battle was the surest measure of a man's state. Some slept where they sat, among the dead, before the field had even been cleared; others walked the camp until dawn. Everyone who had fought knew both conditions and knew which one they had been in. It was not a private matter, since men lay in the open beside each other.
studies.didYouKnow: The same detail, sleep coming over a force around a battle, shows up in the Quran's account of the earlier day at Badr. It is called a security from God there, in almost the same words. Very few bodily experiences are reported twice in the Quran as a sign.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sorts the community by what happened inside them, not by what they did, and it names nobody. The purpose is given at the end: to test what is in the chests and to refine what is in the hearts. A hard day is treated as something that shows what is inward. The sleep of one group becomes a sign only the sleeper can read.

crossReferences.why: Reports the same drowsiness sent down as a security from God, on the earlier day at Badr.
Follows immediately, naming what happened to those who turned back, and the pardon given.
Describes tranquillity sent down into the hearts of believers so that faith would increase.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you do with a night after something has gone badly. Some people sleep and some replay it until morning, and neither is a verdict on anyone's character. But it is information about where you are. Observe yours the next time without judging it, and see what this description sounds like from inside.
studies.explainEasier: After the battle God calmed the believers, and some of them fell asleep right there. Others could only think about themselves and had wrong thoughts about God. God was testing what was really inside them.

studies.title: Some Of What They Earned
studies.meaning: The people who turned back that day are described in one careful sentence. The adversary made them slip, and the reason given is some of what they had earned. That points to an earlier cause without listing it. Then, with nothing in between, the pardon: God has forgiven them. The early scholars note the two names at the close, one about forgiving and one about being slow to anger. They read the second as the unhurried quality that made the pardon possible.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the account of the battle at Uhud. The classical sources report that those who had given way heard this ayah with relief. They were named in it and pardoned in the same breath. The early scholars note that it points to no one by name, and does not say what had been earned earlier. So the description stays general while the comfort stays exact.

keyTerms.note: From the root for slipping on smooth ground. The form implies drawing someone into a slip rather than pushing them, so the fault is shared between the one who slipped and what caused it.
A partitive word, so what is named is only part of what they had earned. The commentators note the restraint of the phrasing, which declines both to specify and to exaggerate.
From a root meaning to be slow to anger and deliberate in judgement. It describes patience in one who has power to act at once, which is why it pairs so naturally with forgiveness.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Running from a battle was the most public failure open to a man in that world. It was remembered, put into poetry, and used against his family for years. There was no way to set it right. That is why an announced pardon was so unusual. It settled in public what would otherwise have followed those men for life.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the second time in a few ayat that the surah says God pardoned the community after the battle. A different word is used each time. One means to wipe away a trace. The other means to cover over. Together they name both the removal of the mark and the covering of the fault.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah does something unusual with blame. In one sentence it names an outside cause, an earlier fault, and a pardon, and none of the three cancels the others. That turns down the choice between blaming a person fully and excusing them fully. The closing name matters too. It describes God as slow and unhurried, and that is what lets an account be settled kindly rather than quickly.

crossReferences.why: Uses a different word for pardon a few ayat earlier, after listing the failures of that day.
Describes the first slip in the same vocabulary, the adversary causing a slipping from a state.
Ends on a similar pairing of pardon and forgiveness, of those with a genuine excuse.

studies.applyIt: There is a difference between an excuse and an account. This ayah gives an account: something pushed, something earlier had weakened the footing, and the whole thing is pardoned. Try describing a failure of yours that way once this week, to yourself, in three parts. Notice that the pardon does not require the first two to be untrue.
studies.explainEasier: Some of you ran away on the day the two armies met. Satan made them slip, because of things they had done before. But God has forgiven them. He forgives, and He is never in a hurry.

studies.title: Had They Stayed With Us
studies.meaning: A sentence people say after a death is quoted and then examined. If they had stayed with us, they would not have died. The ayah does not argue with the logic. It names what the sentence does to the person saying it, making it a wearing regret lodged in their own heart, and then states the fact that undoes it: God gives life and gives death. The early scholars note that the instruction is not to stop grieving but to stop building the version in which the loss did not happen.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, after the battle at Uhud. The community lost many men, and some of their families had been against them going. The early scholars tie the quoted sentence to what was being said in the city afterwards, above all by those who had argued against the march. The Quran gives the saying to a group without naming anyone. It speaks to the believers about the habit, not about the speakers.

keyTerms.gloss: they struck out in the land
keyTerms.note: An idiom for travelling, built on the verb to strike. Arabic pictures a journey as striking the ground with the feet, which makes travel an action taken rather than a passage undergone.
From a root meaning to strip bare and to wear out, used of a camel driven past its strength. It names grief that has consumed the person carrying it rather than sorrow simply felt.
Two verbs in a single clause, both with God as their subject. Setting them together removes the space in which a different arrangement of events could have produced a different outcome.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travel and raiding were the two ways a young man could lift his family's position. Both carried a real chance of not coming back. Every household had weighed it. Relatives who had urged staying home were sometimes proved right in the most painful way. The sentence quoted in this ayah was heard in the streets of Medina for months.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for regret turns up elsewhere in the Quran. There it names a day of wearing regret at the end of all things. Here it is used of something felt now, about a choice already made and past changing. That puts an ordinary grief in the same class as a final one, as the early scholars note.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The harm of the if-only sentence is placed inside the person who holds it. Nothing is said about whether the reasoning holds up. The objection is practical, not logical: the sentence keeps a wound open and nothing can close it. Naming God as the one who gives life and death then takes away what it rests on. The other history it needs was never there to have.

crossReferences.why: Quotes a version of the same sentence from within the community after the battle.
Reports it again a few ayat later, and answers by asking them to avert death from themselves.
Says nothing befalls you but is written, so you do not grieve over what escapes you.

studies.applyIt: Everyone has a sentence beginning with if only, usually about the same event. Say yours out loud once and notice how well practised it is. Then notice that saying it has never once changed anything, and that it costs you something each time. This ayah is not asking you to feel less. It is asking you to stop rehearsing.
studies.explainEasier: When people die, do not talk like those who say they would still be alive if they had stayed home. That kind of talk only leaves regret in your heart. God is the one who gives life and takes it.

studies.title: Better Than What They Gather
studies.meaning: Two short ayat make the same move twice, with the two verbs swapped between them. If you are killed or you die, forgiveness and mercy from God are better than what others are piling up. If you die or you are killed, the gathering is to God. The early scholars note the swap. Each verb stands first once, so neither way of dying is treated as the one that counts. And the thing being compared is what people gather, not staying alive.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, spoken to a community that had just buried many of its own after the battle at Uhud. Others were telling them how much better it would have been to stay home. The early scholars read the comparison at the end of the first ayah as an answer to that argument. What is set against forgiveness and mercy is what people gather, not the lives they keep.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for gathering things together, used of wealth. Its subject is left as a vague they, which keeps the comparison general rather than aimed at anyone in particular.
A different verb, used of driving people together into one place as a herd is gathered. The passive form leaves the gatherer unnamed and the movement entirely unavoidable.
A conditional particle carrying an emphatic oath, so the clause is stronger than a plain if. Both ayat open with it, which is what gives the pair their insistent rhythm.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's estate was counted the day he died, and what he had gathered passed to others within the week. Everyone had watched an inheritance divided. They knew how fast a lifetime of saving became someone else's property. So setting forgiveness against what people pile up was not a far-off comparison. It measured against something they had just seen change hands.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs, dying and being killed, appear in both ayat in opposite order, so each one stands first once. The classical scholars of style treat that kind of swap as a known figure. Here it refuses to rank the two ways of dying against each other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a reward from God against a pile of goods, and it does not compare like with like. What is offered is not survival but forgiveness. What it is measured against is not life but what people gather. That reframes the argument the community was hearing. The choice being urged on them was never between dying and living. It was between two things to want.

crossReferences.why: Continues the theme a few ayat later, saying those killed in God's way are alive with their Lord.
Compares the enjoyment of this world with the hereafter, and calls the first very little.
Says the enjoyment of this world is small, and the hereafter better for one who is mindful.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you are actually comparing when you weigh a risk. Usually it is safety against danger. This passage changes one side of that scale, setting what you would receive against what you are piling up. Try the same change once with a decision you have been avoiding, and see whether the balance sits differently.
studies.explainEasier: If you are killed or you die while serving God, what He gives you is better than anything other people are saving up. Either way, you are going back to God in the end.

studies.title: Gentleness That Held Them Together
studies.meaning: The ayah calls the manner of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) a gift, then draws a consequence from it. Harshness would have emptied the space around him. Three instructions follow, and their order is deliberate. Pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, and then consult them. So the people who had just cost the community a battle are put back into the decisions, not merely excused. Trust is placed after resolve, not instead of it.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This line comes straight after the review of Uhud. The defeat followed a decision taken by consultation, against the Prophet's own first inclination to stay in the city. Archers leaving their post turned an advantage into a rout. The instruction to keep consulting them arrives exactly where consultation had appeared to fail. Early scholars treat that placement as the force of the ayah.

keyTerms.note: From a root used of dough, of pliable wood, of anything that yields under pressure without breaking. The word describes texture rather than mood, so the gentleness is presented as a quality others could feel.
Roughness in manner and word, the opposite of pliable. It is paired here with a second phrase about hardness of heart, separating a harsh way of speaking from the hardness underneath it.
From a root for extracting honey from a comb. Consultation is pictured as drawing out something valuable that is already there, held inside the people being asked.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian tribes were led by consent, not by command. A chief held authority because men chose to follow him. He kept them by hearing their views in assembly and sharing out what came in. He took insult without answering it. A leader who humiliated his followers lost them to another tent by morning. The ayah names that plain political fact, then treats the manner that prevents it as a mercy given from outside.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah moves through several addressees inside one sentence. There is a statement about the Prophet's manner, then three commands given to him, then a closing line about whom God loves. Surah 42 is named after the word for consultation. That exact form occurs only once in the Quran, at 42:38, in a list of the qualities of a believing community.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Character is treated here as revelation's tool, not its ornament. The message would not have held people if the messenger had been abrasive. The ayah says so without embarrassment. It grounds the softness in God's mercy rather than in temperament. It also sets a limit on trust in God by placing it after a decision is made. So reliance is what follows resolve, not a substitute for it.

crossReferences.why: Lists mutual consultation among the marks of a community that answers its Lord.
Describes the same messenger as grieved by their hardship and gentle towards believers.
States plainly that he stands upon a great character, in an early Meccan surah.

studies.applyIt: Before the next decision that affects someone else, ask one person who will have to live with it what they think, and let them finish. You are not required to take the advice. Notice instead what asking does to the room, and to how the decision lands once it is made.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the Prophet that being gentle was a gift. If he had been harsh, people would have walked away. So forgive them, pray for them, and ask them what they think.

studies.title: If God Helps You
studies.meaning: Two conditions are set out in the same shape, and only one of them is comfortable. If God helps you, nobody overcomes you. If He leaves you without support, who will help you after Him. The early scholars note that the second half is a question, not a threat. It asks the hearer to look for another helper and find none. The instruction then follows from both halves together, not from the first alone: so let the believers rely on God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the part that follows the battle at Uhud. Both halves of this ayah had been shown in a single afternoon. The early scholars read the placing as deliberate, since the community had known help and then its loss on the same day. The ayah still states the rule without tying it to that occasion. That is how the surah usually handles such lessons.

keyTerms.note: A verb for abandoning someone at the moment they need help, used of a companion who steps back in a fight. It names withdrawal by someone expected to stand, which is stronger than simply failing to assist.
