An active participle from the root for prevailing. Negating the whole category rather than any particular opponent is what makes the first half absolute rather than comparative.
A command form from the root meaning to appoint an agent to act on your behalf. Reliance in Arabic is a delegation, so it assumes an arrangement made rather than a feeling held.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An agent was a familiar figure in Arabian trade. A merchant who could not travel named someone to buy and sell for him. The deal was plain: the agent acted, and the merchant carried the outcome. The verb this ayah uses for reliance comes straight out of that world. It makes trust an appointment you make, not a mood you hold.
studies.didYouKnow: The call to rely on God comes twice in this surah within a few dozen ayat. One is at the opening of the account of the battle, and this one is at its close. The two of them bracket the whole passage. The wording is the same in both places.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah will not give a guarantee. It gives a place to put the matter instead. Both halves are stated, so being left without support is admitted rather than denied. What follows is reliance, not confidence about how things turn out. That says something exact about trust. It is not a forecast that things will go well. It is a decision about where the matter is placed.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical instruction at the start of this surah's account of the same battle.
Says whoever relies on God, He is sufficient for him, and His command reaches its end.
Says nothing befalls us except what God has written, and closes on the same instruction.

studies.applyIt: The ayah gives you both halves, so do the same. Take something you are anxious about and write two sentences: what it looks like if it goes well, and what it looks like if it does not. Then notice that the conclusion the passage draws comes after both, not after the first one only.
studies.explainEasier: If God is helping you, nobody can beat you. If He leaves you on your own, nobody else can step in and help. So believers put the whole thing in God's hands.

studies.title: Nothing Taken In Secret
studies.meaning: The word at the centre means taking something quietly from what a group has entrusted to you. It points above all at spoils before they are divided. The ayah says this is not something a prophet does. Then it makes the result vivid. Whoever takes will carry what he took to the Day of Resurrection and bring it with him. The early scholars report that the ayah answered a suspicion after the battle about a missing item. They keep more than one account of what it was.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, after the battle at Uhud, where leaving a position had itself been tied to the taking of spoils. The classical sources report a suspicion going round about something missing from the collected goods. They read the ayah as an answer to it. Reports of the item itself differ, so the early scholars treat the occasion as clear in outline and unsure in its details.

keyTerms.note: A precise term for removing something from common property before it is distributed. Arabic has a dedicated word for it, which tells you how familiar the problem was in that society.

keyTerms.gloss: he will bring what he took
keyTerms.note: The verb is to come or arrive, so the image is of a person carrying the item into the gathering. Nothing is said about its weight, and the commentators note that the carrying is the point.
The commercial verb used earlier in this surah for a debt discharged completely. Its reappearance places both the taking and the reckoning in the vocabulary of accounts kept and settled.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Spoils were gathered into one place and shared out by an agreed method. The whole system rested on nothing leaving the pile first. A man who took an item early gained something small and put the whole arrangement at risk. Everyone knew that. Everyone also knew how easy it was to do in the confusion after a fight.
studies.didYouKnow: Arabic has its own verb for taking from common property before it is shared out. It is not the ordinary word for theft. The Quran uses it only in this surah. That a word exists just for this shows how much a fair division of spoils mattered to holding a fighting force together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a suspicion by stating a rule about prophets, not by denying one charge. That method is worth noting. It makes the defence a matter of what a prophet is, not of one man's word. The picture of carrying the item into the gathering does something too. A hidden act becomes an object you can see. That is how the Quran usually shows a covered thing being uncovered at last.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the division of spoils directly, referring the whole matter to God and the Messenger.
Instructs that trusts be rendered back to those they belong to, and that judgement be just.
Uses the same verb for being paid in full, of every soul on a day beyond any doubt.

studies.applyIt: The specific failure here is taking a little from something held in common: an expense claim, a shared resource, time billed but not worked. It is always small, which is exactly why it is easy. Pick one such thing and put it back this week, quietly. Nobody needs to know, which is rather the point.
studies.explainEasier: A prophet would never take things in secret. Anyone who does will have to carry what he took on the Day when everyone stands up again. Then each person gets exactly what he earned, with nothing taken away.

studies.title: Not The Same At All
studies.meaning: A question is asked that answers itself. Is the one who went after God's approval like the one who came away carrying His anger. Then a very short ayah, easy to pass over. They are degrees with God. The wording is unusual. It does not say they have degrees; it says they are degrees. The early scholars read that as making people one with their rank, rather than having a rank handed to them from outside.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the section that follows the battle at Uhud. What people did on that single day had varied a great deal. The early scholars tie the pairing to it, since the passage comes straight after a line about taking from the spoils. The question and the words about degrees are read together. They name differences the day itself had made plain.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form of the word for contentment, used earlier in this surah among the rewards of the mindful. It names the giver's regard rather than any particular gift given.
The verb means to return bearing something, used of a traveller coming home with a load. Displeasure is described as something carried back rather than as something sent after a person.
The plural of a word for a step on a stair. Saying that people are degrees rather than have them collapses the distinction between a person and their standing entirely.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rank in Arabian society came from birth, from wealth and from the name of your line. You could see it in where a man sat and when he spoke. Everyone knew the order in a gathering. An ayah saying that people are their own degrees before God cut across all of that. In that world standing was inherited, not built by anything you did.
studies.didYouKnow: The wording that people are degrees, rather than that they have them, turns up in a similar form elsewhere in the Quran. The early scholars of grammar ask whether a word has been left out. Most read the gap as meant. The shorter form ties the person to the rank more tightly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats standing before God as something a person becomes, not something handed out. That is what the odd grammar does. It fits the surah's argument that a hard day showed what people already were. The two paths matter too. One is named by what it goes after. The other is named by what it comes back carrying.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same construction of the believers, saying they are degrees with their Lord.
Names God's approval earlier in this surah, among the things better than what is loved here.
Says for all there are degrees according to what they did, and God is not unaware.

studies.applyIt: The question here is rhetorical, which means it expects you to answer it. Take one thing you did this week and ask honestly which of the two descriptions fits: pursuing approval, or coming away carrying something. Most days contain both. Naming which was which is the whole exercise, and it takes a minute.
studies.explainEasier: A person who goes after what pleases God is not the same as a person who ends up with God angry at him. They are not on the same level. God sees exactly what each one does.

studies.title: A Messenger From Among Themselves
studies.meaning: The favour is named and then unpacked in three verbs. A messenger was raised from among the people themselves, and he recites the signs to them, purifies them, and teaches them the Book and wisdom. The phrase about being from among themselves carries weight, since it makes the messenger a neighbour rather than a visitor. The ayah closes by naming what came before, described plainly as evident straying, with nothing softened.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, set inside the account of what followed the battle at Uhud. The early scholars note where it falls. A community that had just failed is reminded of what it was given, not of what it did. The three tasks listed here also appear in Abraham's prayer over the sanctuary in an earlier surah. The scholars read this ayah as the answer to that prayer.

keyTerms.note: A verb for granting a benefit, from a root also connected with cutting off. In its good sense it names an unearned gift, and the Quran uses it of favours nobody could have claimed as a right.
Literally from their souls. The phrase makes the messenger one of them in origin and in kind, not merely present among them, which is what the commentators draw out of it.
From a root covering both purity and increase. It names cleansing and growth as one process, so what is removed and what develops are described by a single verb.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Authority in Arabia was local. A man listened to someone whose family he knew, whose lineage he could recite, and whose conduct he had watched over years. An outsider carried no weight whatever he said. Being from among themselves was therefore not a detail of biography; it was the precondition for anyone being heard at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The three tasks named here are reciting, purifying and teaching. The same three appear in the prayer Abraham makes over the sanctuary in an earlier surah. He asks that a messenger be raised from among them to do exactly these things. The early scholars read the two passages as request and answer, and note that the order is different.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation here comes through someone the people knew, not through an event nobody could relate to. That changes how it is taken in. The three things named are ordinary and can be repeated: reciting, purifying, teaching. The ayah also calls what came before plain straying, with nothing added to soften it. That keeps the favour from being read as something the community had earned.

crossReferences.why: Records Abraham's prayer for a messenger who would do these same three things.
Repeats the same three functions almost word for word, of a community without scripture.
Describes the messenger as from among yourselves, grieved by whatever distresses you.

studies.applyIt: Notice the order in this ayah: recited to, purified, then taught. Most people try to run it backwards and start with learning. Try a week on the first item instead. Read a short passage aloud often, without studying it. Then see whether the third one lands differently.
studies.explainEasier: God did the believers a great kindness. He sent them a messenger who was one of their own people. He reads them God's words, makes them clean, and teaches them the Book. Before that they were clearly lost.

studies.title: It Is From Yourselves
studies.meaning: A question is quoted and answered in four words. After a disaster the community asks how this happened, when they had dealt out twice as much on an earlier day. The answer is short and not flattering: it is from your own selves. Then the next ayah says the same event came by God's leave, and names what it was for. The early scholars hold both statements together. What the people did and what God allowed describe one event from two angles, not two rival explanations.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the account of the battle at Uhud. The comparison points back to the earlier day at Badr, where the losses on the other side were roughly double what the community suffered here. The early scholars note that the question quoted was asked in earnest. A community helped once could not see why it had not been helped again.

keyTerms.note: From the verb to hit a target, so a calamity is named by its accuracy rather than by its size. The same root runs through this surah's whole vocabulary for what befalls people.
A dual construction meaning double, referring back to the losses inflicted at the earlier battle. Its presence is what makes the question reasonable rather than merely petulant.
Literally from with yourselves, a phrase for something originating in a place rather than merely being located there. It names the source of what happened, not just where it landed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tribes kept exact counts of their losses. Everyone knew how many had fallen on each side of a fight, and those numbers set what was owed and where a feud stood. So the comparison this ayah makes was one the audience could check. That is part of why the question felt so pressing to them.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one after it give two different answers to the same question. One names what the people did. The other names God's leave. The Quran sets them side by side without smoothing them together. The early scholars treat that pairing as the answer, not as a problem to be solved.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage lays responsibility on the people without taking the event out of God's hands. It does that simply by stating both. So neither easy way out is open: blaming the circumstances, or using a decree as an excuse. The purpose named in the second ayah, that the believers be known, also puts the disaster to work. That changes what it was rather than explaining it away.

crossReferences.why: States the principle more generally: good reaching you is from God, and ill from yourself.
Says whatever strikes you is for what your own hands earned, and much is pardoned.
Gives the detailed account of what came from themselves on that particular day.

studies.applyIt: The community here asks a fair question and gets a short answer. Notice that the answer holds no comfort. Comfort comes later in the passage, not instead of it. Next time something goes wrong, answer the how question honestly first. Then go looking for the comfort.
studies.explainEasier: When you were hit hard, you asked how this could happen, even though you had hit them twice as hard before. The answer is that it came from you. God let it happen so it would show who really believes.

studies.title: Said With Their Mouths
studies.meaning: A group is described by an invitation and by their answer to it. They were told to come and fight, or else to defend. They replied that if they knew how to fight they would have followed. The ayah does not argue with the excuse. It observes where they stood that day, then states something general: they say with their mouths what is not in their hearts. The early scholars note the closing clause. It says God knows better what they hide, without naming what it was.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the account of the battle at Uhud, where a large part of the force turned back before the fighting. The classical sources describe an exchange on the road: they were urged to keep going and refused. The Quran reports their words and its own judgement without naming anyone. The early scholars keep to that same restraint.

keyTerms.note: From a root associated with a burrow having two exits, used of a creature that enters by one and leaves by the other. The image is of an arrangement built for escape rather than for dwelling.
A verb for repelling something, offered here as an alternative to fighting. Its presence widens the invitation, so the refusal cannot be read as declining one particular role.
A comparative rather than an identification. The ayah says they were nearer to refusal than to faith on that day, which is a measurement of distance rather than a verdict about a category.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Excuses on the road were common and mostly accepted. A man could turn back for a sick relative, a debt, or a doubt about the plan, and nobody usually pressed him. The excuse quoted here is a different kind. It claims not knowing how, rather than a duty at home. Anyone who knew these men would have seen through it.
studies.didYouKnow: The root behind the word for playing a double part is linked in Arabic with a burrow that has a second opening. A small desert animal digs it that way so it can escape if the first is blocked. The early Arabic dictionary writers keep that picture. It shapes the term: not a lie, but an exit made ready in advance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage measures instead of labelling. It says that on that day they were nearer to one thing than to another. That leaves the position open and names a direction rather than a fixed state. Its last move is the one the surah makes elsewhere. What they hid is not spelled out, and knowing it is left to God. That stops a description from turning into an accusation.

crossReferences.why: Quotes another excuse for staying behind, saying their tongues say what is not in their hearts.
Describes a journey declined, with an excuse the passage says they knew to be untrue.
Describes another group on the same day, preoccupied with themselves and concealing their thoughts.

studies.applyIt: The excuse quoted here claims inability rather than unwillingness, which is the most common shape an excuse takes. Listen for it in your own next few days: I would, but I do not know how. Sometimes it is true. Notice one occasion this week where it is the polite version of something else.
studies.explainEasier: Some men were told to come and fight for God, or at least help hold the enemy back. They said they would have come if they knew how to fight. That was not true. God knows what people keep hidden inside.

studies.title: Do Not Suppose Them Dead
studies.meaning: The passage answers a taunt. Those who stayed home said the dead would be living had they listened, and the reply is a challenge rather than an argument: keep death away from yourselves, if what you say is true. Then a direct correction of how the reader is to think of the fallen. They are not dead, they are with their Lord and provided for, which places them in the present tense.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina, after the battle of Uhud. A body of men turned back before the fighting, and afterwards said of the dead that they would have lived had they taken the same advice. Early scholars identify these ayat with that remark. Some seventy of the community were killed that day. Nearly every household in Medina had lost someone or was tending someone wounded.

keyTerms.note: A verb for repelling something advancing at you, used of pushing back a flood or an attacker. Turning it towards death makes the challenge physical, as if the claim were about a force that could be blocked.
The plain word for living people, not a softened term. It is given without qualification, and early scholars are careful to say the life meant is real while its manner is not disclosed.
A passive verb in the ongoing present, the same word used of daily sustenance in this world. It answers the practical anxiety of families left behind about people they can no longer feed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The dead of Uhud were buried on the field, two and three to a grave, in the clothes they fell in. Their families could walk out to the hill from Medina in an hour, and did. Widows and mothers had lost the men who brought in the harvest and defended the wells. Grief in that society was public and loud, with formal mourning that could run for months.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran twice corrects the language used of those killed in God's cause, here and at 2:154. The wording differs. This passage rules out supposing them dead; the earlier one rules out saying it. That earlier passage also adds that the reader has no perception of the life in question.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The taunt assumes that staying out of danger is what keeps a person alive, and the reply does not argue the point. It hands the claim back as a test the speakers cannot pass, which is a way of showing that the assumption was never really believed. The second ayah then relocates the question. Whether someone is alive turns out not to be settled by what those watching can see.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same correction earlier in the Quran, adding that the living are simply not perceived.
Continues the Uhud review, answering people who thought staying home would have changed the outcome.
Answers the same instinct: death reaches people wherever they are, even in fortified towers.

studies.applyIt: If you have lost someone, try saying their name today in the present tense in one ordinary sentence, the way you would speak of a person who has travelled. The ayah is not asking you to feel less. It is asking you to notice how much of grief is built on a tense you chose without thinking.
studies.explainEasier: Some people who stayed home said the dead would still be alive if they had listened. God answers: then stop your own death, if you can. Those killed for God are not dead. They are alive with Him.

studies.title: Glad For Those Behind Them
studies.meaning: The description carries on from the ayah before, and the striking thing is which way the attention runs. They delight in what they have been given. Then they are glad for those who have not yet joined them, the ones still behind. Their joy is not for themselves alone. It reaches back to people still living. The early scholars note the verb for receiving good news, which is used twice across the two ayat.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the passage about those killed at the battle of Uhud, spoken to a community burying its own. The early scholars read this section as comfort for the bereaved, since it describes the dead as taken up with those left behind. That direction is what the sources stress. Grief usually runs the other way.

keyTerms.note: A participle from the root for gladness, sometimes used in the Quran of a gladness that turns into vanity. Here it takes God's bounty as its object, which fixes the sense securely.
A form of the verb for glad tidings that implies seeking or welcoming it. It names the reception of news rather than its announcement, which is why it suits those already arrived.

keyTerms.gloss: does not let go to waste
keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to lose or misplace something. It denies loss rather than promising increase, which is a quieter reassurance than a promise and a more exact one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The dead were buried quickly, often on the field itself, and families frequently never saw the body. What relatives wanted most was news: how he died, whether he suffered, whether he was afraid. Messengers carried such accounts back to the city and were pressed for detail. These ayat arrive into a community waiting for exactly that kind of report.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase saying they will have no fear and will not grieve comes up again and again in the Quran, always of those in God's care. It appears more than a dozen times across many surahs. Here it is said not of the dead themselves, but of the living they are glad about.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The dead are described as still attentive to the living, which turns the usual shape of grief around. The bereaved are being told that the people they mourn are glad about them. The passage also closes on a denial rather than a promise. It says the reward is not lost. That meets the exact fear of a community whose effort had just ended in a setback.

crossReferences.why: Opens this passage, saying not to think those killed in God's way are dead.
Says the same thing more briefly, that they are alive though you do not perceive it.
Closes the surah with the same assurance that no worker's work is allowed to go to waste.

studies.applyIt: Notice which way the attention runs here: from those who have arrived, back toward those still travelling. If you are grieving someone, try holding that direction for a moment rather than the usual one. You do not have to believe anything new to try it. See what changes in the shape of the missing.
studies.explainEasier: They are happy with what God has given them. They are also happy for the ones they left behind, who have not come yet. Those people have nothing to fear and nothing to be sad about. God will not waste what they did.

studies.title: They Answered While Wounded
studies.meaning: A group is described by one action taken at the worst possible moment. They answered the call of God and the Messenger after the wound had already reached them. The ayah says nothing about what they did next. The answering itself is the whole of the praise. Then the reward is tied to two qualities rather than to the act: doing well, and being mindful of God. The early scholars read that as widening the promise beyond that group, to a state anyone could be in.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources tie this ayah to the day after the battle at Uhud, when the community was called out again to follow the force that was pulling away. Many who answered were wounded from the day before. The march ended without any fighting. The sources note that, since the praise attaches to the answering rather than to a battle.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb to respond that implies answering a summons. It names the reply rather than what followed it, which is why the commendation can rest on the response alone.
The same word used earlier in this surah of the wound that reached both sides. Its reappearance ties this ayah directly to the account of the battle rather than leaving the setting general.
From the root for beauty and excellence, so doing well means doing something finely rather than merely correctly. The Quran uses it of a quality of action rather than a quantity of action.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wounds in that world were treated with whatever was at hand: cautery, honey, cloth. A man cut the day before could barely hold a shield, and everyone knew it. Setting out again with untreated injuries was visible to the whole city, because the column left in daylight. The praise here describes something the community actually watched.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical sources report that the march this ayah refers to ended with no fighting at all. The other force had already moved on. So the praise goes to men who set out wounded and came back having done nothing. Few places in the Quran praise a response so clearly apart from its result.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage splits the worth of an act from what it achieved, praising a response that produced nothing. Then it goes further. The reward is tied to qualities rather than to the episode, so the praise is not shut up with the men who went. A piece of historical praise does not become a closed record. It turns into a description anyone can fit.

crossReferences.why: Continues the account, giving the words those who answered said when warned about the enemy.
Describes earlier communities who did not weaken at what struck them in God's way.
Says nothing suffered on such a journey is lost, but is written as a good deed for them.

studies.applyIt: The praise here is for showing up wounded and achieving nothing. If you have been waiting to feel recovered before returning to something you value, notice that this ayah does not wait for that. Go back this week in whatever state you are in, and let the response itself be the whole of the act.
studies.explainEasier: These people answered God and the Messenger even after they had been hurt. They went out again while they were still sore and tired. God has a great reward for the ones among them who do good and stay careful of Him.

studies.title: God Is Enough For Us
studies.meaning: Fear is offered to them as information, and it has the opposite effect. The report is accurate. An army has gathered. Their response is not to deny the danger but to change what the danger is measured against. The two words they answer with are a reckoning and a title: God suffices, and He is the best one to entrust affairs to. Early scholars note that their faith increased rather than merely held.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This refers to the days just after Uhud, when the wounded were called out again to follow the withdrawing Meccan army. Early scholars connect the ayah with warnings brought to the Muslims that a larger force was gathering to finish them. Reports differ on who carried the warning. So the ayah is usually read for the response it records rather than for the messenger.

keyTerms.note: From the root for counting and reckoning. The word does not say God will help; it says the account already balances, so nothing further needs to be added to the side they are on.

keyTerms.gloss: the trustee, the one relied on
keyTerms.note: A term from ordinary business for the agent you hand your affairs to and whose decisions bind you. Calling God this puts reliance in the vocabulary of delegation rather than of feeling.
Placed as the object of a verb meaning to increase, so faith is treated as a quantity that can rise and fall. The grammar assumes a thing with degrees, not a line that is either crossed or not.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: News in Arabia travelled by rider and by rumour. A caravan arriving from the north could carry a report that changed a town's plans by evening. There was no way to check a claim about an army two days away except by sending men towards it. Whole settlements decided on the strength of one traveller's word. That is why the standing of the person speaking mattered so much.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical commentaries keep a report from Ibn Abbas. He said this same sentence was spoken by Abraham when he was thrown into the fire, and again by the community on the occasion of this ayah. The words occur in this exact form only here. The root turns up across the Quran with other pronouns.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reliance is presented as a judgement, not a mood. The believers do not report feeling calm. They state a sufficiency and give God a title drawn from law and trade. That makes trust something a frightened person can perform without first becoming unafraid. The passage also lets fear be a real report about real danger, and puts the change entirely in what the danger is set against.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same fear from the other side, that nothing reaches a person outside what God has written.
Uses the same word for sufficiency, promising that God is enough for whoever relies on Him.
Addresses the Prophet with the same construction, God is enough for you and those who follow.

studies.applyIt: Next time bad news arrives, notice the gap between the report and your reaction to it, and put one sentence in that gap before you do anything else. It does not have to be long. The point is that the danger and your response are two separate things, and only one of them is yours.
studies.explainEasier: People told them a big army was coming and tried to scare them. It made them trust God more instead. They said: God is enough for us, and He is the best one to look after us.

studies.title: Fear Me, Not Them
studies.meaning: The passage closes an episode rather than opening one. Those who marched out despite their injuries came home with favour and profit, untouched, having pursued what pleases God. Then the frame widens. The intimidation they faced is attributed not to the enemy but to Satan, working through people who follow him. What follows is a redirection rather than a denial. Fear is not abolished; it is pointed somewhere else. Scholars read the clause about Satan and his allies in more than one way.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the aftermath of the fighting at Uhud. The early scholars connect these ayat to the march the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) called for immediately afterwards, when wounded men went out again to a halt on the Mecca road and the opposing army did not return. Other reports connect them to an appointed meeting near Badr the following year that was not kept. Both settings fit the wording.

keyTerms.note: From a root for satisfaction and acceptance. It names not a gift given but God being pleased, which the classical commentators treat as the highest thing the Quran promises, above the gardens themselves.

An intensive form of the verb to fear: to work fear into someone. The object is read differently by different commentators, either that he frightens you of his allies or that he makes his own followers fearful.
A wide word covering injury, misfortune and wrong together. Its indefinite form under a negation sweeps the whole category, so the claim is that not one instance of harm reached them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rumour travelled the Hijaz faster than any army. A traveller arriving at a Medinan well could say that Mecca had regrouped and was coming back, and by evening every household knew. There was no way to check. Families with wounded men had to decide overnight whether to send them out again on the strength of a stranger's word. This passage describes that kind of night.
studies.didYouKnow: The opening words here repeat, exactly, a phrase used three ayat earlier at 3:171. In the earlier place it describes what those killed at Uhud rejoice in; here it describes what the survivors came home with. The same short phrase carries a promise in one line and its fulfilment in the other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage splits fear in two. One kind answers power you can see and count. The other is owed to a power you cannot. By naming the first as Satan's work, it treats being frightened as something done to a person, not as a plain fact about their situation. And it makes the second kind of fear a mark of belief. Courage and faith end up on one footing, instead of courage being left to a person's nature.

crossReferences.why: Records what the believers said when the same rumour reached them, immediately before this passage.
Calls the scheming of Satan weak, which is the other half of the claim made here about his allies.
Describes messengers who fear no one but God, the same redirection of fear stated as a rule.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time a piece of news makes your chest tighten, and before acting on it ask who is telling you and what they gain by your alarm. Most frightening reports arrive with no way to check them. You do not have to talk yourself out of the feeling. Just hold it for an hour before you let it decide anything.
studies.explainEasier: They came home safe, with good things from God, and nothing bad had touched them. They had gone after what pleases God. It was only Satan trying to make them afraid of his friends. Do not fear them. Fear God.

studies.title: Not Yours To Grieve Over
studies.meaning: Two sentences addressed to someone watching others fall away, and both refuse the assumption underneath the grief. Speed is the image: they are racing into denial, as if hurrying. The reply is that nothing they do reaches God. What is actually at stake is their own portion of what comes after. The second ayah puts it as a trade, faith handed over and its opposite received, which makes the loss theirs and gives it a price.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the stretch after the setback at Uhud. The strain showed up people who had joined the community without really believing, and who now moved away openly. The early scholars read the address as comfort for the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), whose grief over refusal is described elsewhere in the Quran. No single occasion is reported with confidence. The setting is a community sorting itself out under pressure.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb to hurry that carries the sense of competing. The identical word appears at 3:114 for people who race towards good deeds, so one image serves two opposite directions.

A word from the language of division: the portion that falls to someone when something is shared out. It treats the Hereafter as an estate in which everyone present has an allotment, and says theirs is empty.
Commercial vocabulary. The verb means to purchase, so denial is what they paid for and faith is what they handed over. The Quran uses this trading frame repeatedly for choices that cannot be undone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina's market ran mostly on swaps rather than coin: dates for cloth, a camel against a debt. Everyone knew the feeling of making a trade and seeing later what they had given up. Traders argued about whether one swap had been fair for days afterwards. Putting belief in that language let a listener feel the deal in his hands instead of thinking about it from far off.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for racing appears earlier in this same surah, at 3:114, in exactly the same grammatical form. There it describes people who hurry towards good works and are praised for it. The word itself is neutral; only the direction of travel differs, and the surah lets the two lines stand a few pages apart.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says plainly that people's refusal does no damage to God. That sounds obvious, and it clears away a whole kind of worry. If turning away cannot hurt the one turned away from, then standing up for religion is not the rescue of someone weak. It also draws a line under what the watcher is answerable for. Grief that assumes you could have stopped another person's choice is grief about something that was never yours.

crossReferences.why: Names the same grief and its intensity, warning the Prophet not to destroy himself over people's refusal.
Uses the same buying image for the same exchange, and adds that the transaction returned nothing.
States the asymmetry underneath this passage: the need runs one way, so refusal costs God nothing.

studies.applyIt: Pick one person whose choices have been weighing on you. Say plainly to yourself which part of it was ever in your hands and which part was not. Then do the small thing that is still yours, a message or an invitation or one honest sentence, and stop at the edge of what you can actually reach.
studies.explainEasier: Do not be sad about people who rush to turn away from God. They cannot hurt God at all. They are giving up faith and taking something worthless in its place. A painful punishment is waiting for them.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Long Life Is Not Approval
studies.meaning: The ayah answers a conclusion people draw from what they can see. Someone denies God and does well, and the delay looks like approval. The passage grants the delay and rejects that reading. Extra time is not a reward. It makes the record longer. The early scholars are careful with the clause about increase, noting that Arabic can use this form for a result rather than for a purpose. The last word calls the punishment humiliating, not just painful.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, among the passages after Uhud that speak to the community's confidence while its opponents looked untouched. Mecca's leaders had gone home whole, and their trade went on. The early scholars report no particular occasion. They place the ayah inside a running argument about how to read success in this world. The surah picks that argument up again at its close, warning about being impressed by wealth.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to extend time and to let out slack. Arabic used it of a tether paid out to a grazing animal, so the picture is of rope given rather than of a penalty cancelled.

An emphatic negative of the verb to reckon or calculate. It addresses a conclusion someone has worked out for themselves, which is why the reply corrects an inference rather than answering a stated claim.
Built from the root for lowliness, it names punishment that shames rather than only hurts. Three consecutive ayat here close with the same noun for torment and three different adjectives.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A debtor in Arabia could be given more time, and a creditor who put the date back was doing a favour with a limit on it. Everyone understood that a delayed debt was still a debt. An extension could turn into a trap if the debtor kept borrowing inside it. Listeners had watched families sink further during a grace period they had asked for themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: From 176 to 178, the same word for torment closes three ayat in a row. Each time a different adjective follows it: great, then painful, then humiliating. The other end of the surah is built the same way. The two ayat that promise reward, 195 and 198, each close with a noun, then the phrase from God, then a clause about what is with Him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah will not let what you can see stand as a verdict. That protects two people at once. It stops the comfortable from reading their comfort as approval. It stops the struggling from reading hardship as rejection. It also treats time as neutral rather than kind: what a person does with an extra ten years decides what those years were. Judgement is put off here, not called off.

crossReferences.why: Asks the same question about wealth and children and gives the same answer, that extension is not favour.
Names the gradual drawing-on this ayah describes, and adds that the delay is deliberate.
Sets the same brief enjoyment against what follows it, compressed into a single short sentence.

studies.applyIt: Think of an area of your life where nothing has gone wrong for a long time. Try not to read that as a verdict on how you are living. Ask instead what the last quiet year was used for. Name one thing you would do differently if this stretch of ease were a loan of time rather than a wage.
studies.explainEasier: People who turn away from God sometimes get a long, easy run. That is not God being pleased with them. The extra time only lets them pile up more wrong. In the end a shameful punishment is waiting for them.

studies.title: The Sorting You Cannot See
studies.meaning: Two denials with a single point between them. The community will not be left undifferentiated; events will separate what is sound from what is spoiled. But the separating happens through what people do, and nobody is handed a list. Knowledge of what is hidden stays with God, and where any of it is given out it goes to messengers He selects. So the sorting is real, and its results are not visible to the people being sorted. The ayah ends by asking for belief rather than for information.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately after Uhud, where the battle had done exactly what the ayah describes. Men who marched out turned back before the fighting; others held their ground and were killed. The early scholars read the ayah as an answer to the wish that the insincere had been identified in advance, which would have spared the community its losses. The reply is that the identification is what the events were for.

keyTerms.note: The verb for sorting a mixed heap into its kinds, used of grain and of coins. It assumes the two are already different and merely mixed together, so the sorting reveals rather than creates.
A word for what is clean, pleasant and fit to use, applied to food, water and land. Its opposite here means foul or spoiled, so the pair is drawn from produce rather than from law.
Everything absent from perception, not only the future. With the definite article it names a whole domain rather than a single fact, which is why the denial concerns access and not any one item.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Threshing was a sorting job everyone had watched. Grain was beaten loose from the stalk, thrown up into the wind and let fall, and what was light blew away while what was heavy landed in a heap. Nobody could tell by looking at an unthreshed sheaf what proportion of it was chaff. The work of separating was the only way to find out, and it needed a wind.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah changes person in the middle of a single clause. It speaks of the believers from outside, in the third person, and then without a break says what you are upon. Arabic rhetoric has a name for this turn and treats it as a way of pulling listeners inside a sentence that began as a description of somebody else.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage pulls apart two things people often run together. God knows who is sincere. That does not mean anyone else can. The first is granted fully and the second is denied flatly, and that denial is what makes suspicion useless between people. It also gives hardship a job that is neither punishment nor accident. Difficulty is how a claim turns into a fact.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same principle as a question: whether people expect their claim of faith to go untested.
States the same reservation of the unseen, with the same exception made for a chosen messenger.
Uses the identical phrase about separating the foul from the good, in the setting of another battle.

studies.applyIt: Think of a stretch of difficulty you are in now, and ask what it is sorting rather than what it is punishing. Do not answer for anyone else. Write one line about something that has become clearer to you about yourself since it began: a habit you did not know you had, a fear you had not named.
studies.explainEasier: God will not leave the believers all mixed together. Hard days show who is true and who is not. He does not hand you a list of what is hidden. He tells His messengers what He wants them to know.

studies.title: Collared With What You Kept
studies.meaning: The ayah corrects a sum people do in their heads. Holding back feels like keeping, so it reads as gain. The passage says it is loss. Then it gives the picture that makes the loss visible: what was hoarded is fastened round the neck on the Day of Resurrection. The early scholars differ on whether the collar is the wealth itself changed, or a punishment shaped like it. The closing clause takes away the whole premise. God inherits the heavens and the earth, so nothing was ever held for good.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The long section dealing with the aftermath of Uhud turns here to money, and the early scholars read the ayah broadly rather than tying it to one episode. Some connect it to withholding knowledge of earlier scripture rather than wealth, since the ayat immediately following address concealment. Others keep it general. Medina at this point was under real strain, with an immigrant population living on the resources of its hosts.

keyTerms.note: The verb names a settled disposition rather than a single act: a standing reluctance to let go. The ayah attaches it not to wealth in general but specifically to what God gave them of His bounty.
Built from the word for a neck-ring. The same root gives the word for what a person is able to bear, so the image is of a burden fastened where it cannot be set down.
The term from estate law for what passes to heirs when someone dies. Applied to the heavens and the earth it turns every owner into a temporary holder and God into the one who remains.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Medina was mostly visible and mostly heavy: date palms, grain stores, camels, silver weighed out. A household's standing could be read from its walled garden. Hoarding was therefore not a private act, since neighbours could see which stores never moved. Burial was quick and plain, so the distance between a full storehouse and a wrapped body was something people had watched close within a single day.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical collections keep a report from the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). In it, hoarded wealth comes on the Day of Resurrection as a serpent that seizes the man who kept it, and this ayah is recited as its basis. The picture is already in the wording. The verb here is built on the word for a ring worn at the neck.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah treats ownership as a claim that reality does not support. What a person has is described as given, and the final clause names God as the one to whom everything reverts. Between those two statements, hoarding looks less like a moral failing than a mistake about the facts. Notice that no instruction to give is issued. What is dismantled is the reasoning that makes holding on feel prudent.

crossReferences.why: Extends the same picture, with hoarded metal heated and applied to the body that kept it.
Traces stinginess back to the assumption of self-sufficiency that this ayah's closing clause removes.
Names people as successors to what they hold, the same relation implied by the inheritance clause here.

studies.applyIt: Look at one thing you are holding that you have not used in a year: money set aside for no purpose, a tool, a coat. Do not resolve to become generous. Just decide today where that single item goes, and move it this week. The point is the specific object, not the feeling you have about it.
studies.explainEasier: Some people hold back the good things God gave them and think that is best for them. It is not. What they held on to will be hung round their necks on the Day when everyone rises.

studies.title: A Sentence God Heard
studies.meaning: The passage begins with hearing, not with a reply. A remark was made, that God is the needy one and its speakers the wealthy. The first response is simply that it was heard. Then the remark is joined to something far older, the killing of prophets. The two are treated as one turn of mind separated by centuries, not as two unrelated crimes. The closing line shuts off any complaint about the sentence. What is met is what the hands sent ahead.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The early scholars connect the remark to a taunt made in the city, aimed at the Quran's way of describing charity as a loan given to God. They do not agree on the exact wording or on who was there. They record it as one particular occasion rather than a general description. The ayat around it carry on a long argument with those in Medina who held earlier scripture.

keyTerms.note: The plain past tense, placed first in the sentence for weight. The reply to a remark made in private is not an argument but a statement that it arrived, which changes what kind of thing the remark was.

The verb for entering something in a register or a contract. Its future prefix makes the recording a promise, so the words are handled as an entry to be produced later rather than an insult to be answered now.

An intensive form, not the ordinary word for unjust. The classical commentators discuss the force of the intensive here and read the denial as ruling out injustice altogether rather than only its extreme degree.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation in Medina was made and unmade by things said in courtyards. A cutting line about a rival could cross the town before the evening meal, and poets were paid to make them. Nothing could be taken back once enough people had heard it. Feuds were kept alive for generations by single sentences nobody had ever written down.
studies.didYouKnow: The whole of the second ayah here appears again, word for word, at 8:51. A slightly changed form of it appears at 22:10. The phrase denying that God wrongs His servants uses the same strong grammatical form everywhere it occurs. In every case it stands at the very end of an ayah, never inside one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two claims are set against each other. The remark treats need as something that could attach to God, and the passage does not argue the point; it records it. What follows says more. Connecting a sentence spoken in Medina to the killing of prophets centuries earlier treats contempt as continuous across time. And the final denial makes the record, rather than any verdict imposed from outside, the thing that decides.

crossReferences.why: Contains the language of lending to God that the commentators say this remark was answering.
Reports a similar saying about God and handles it the same way, quoting it before replying.
Joins the same two charges, a saying about God and the killing of prophets, in one sentence.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you said about God in a bad week, out loud or only in your head. The passage's point is that it was heard, not that it was unforgivable. Say the truer sentence now, in your own words, without deleting the first one. Notice how differently the two sit in the same mouth.
studies.explainEasier: God heard the people who said that He was poor and they were rich. Their words are being written down, along with the prophets they killed. What they get in the end is what their own hands sent ahead.

studies.title: The Sign They Asked For
studies.meaning: A condition is quoted and then pulled apart by its own history. The demand is for one particular sign: an offering that fire comes down and eats up. It is presented as something already agreed with God. The reply does not deny that such signs were ever given. It grants them, and asks what happened to the messengers who brought them. The argument turns on a fact, not a rule. The condition had been met before, and the outcome was killing. So the condition was never the real obstacle.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside a long exchange with those in the city who held earlier scripture. The sign named was known from their tradition, where fire coming down on an offering marked that it was accepted. The early scholars treat this as a demand reported from particular speakers, not a general one, and no single occasion is agreed. They read the reply as aimed at the argument itself, not at any person.

keyTerms.note: The verb for entering a binding agreement, used of treaties between tribes. Placing it here makes the demand sound like an obligation already contracted rather than a preference, which is why the reply goes after its history.
From the root meaning to draw near. The word names the offering by its purpose, closeness, rather than by what is offered, and it occurs only three times in the whole Quran.
Plural of a word for whatever makes a thing evident. It covers miracles, arguments and plain scripture together, so the reply refuses to concede that only one kind of sign should count.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sacrifice was ordinary and public. An animal was brought, killed and shared out, and everyone there could see whether it met the standards of their own tradition. So setting a visible test for a prophet was not a strange request. It asked for the kind of proof a market or a tribal meeting used every day, put to a question neither could settle.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for an offering occurs three times in the Quran and nowhere else. One is in the account of the two sons of Adam at 5:27. There two offerings are brought and only one is accepted. The other is at 46:28. There it names not an offering at all, but the gods people took as a way of drawing near.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage turns down a familiar move: setting a condition for belief that is really a way of putting it off. It grants that the sign was given, then points at what followed. That makes the demand defeat itself, without denying that God gives signs. What it implies is that resistance to a message is rarely about evidence. Whoever names a proof will usually find another reason once it comes.

crossReferences.why: States the general principle this ayah argues from one case, that supplied proof does not compel belief.
Records the same pattern of messengers denied and killed that the reply here appeals to.
Lists a similar set of conditions set for a messenger, and the answer he was told to give.

studies.applyIt: Notice a condition you have set for yourself: the point at which you will start praying properly, or reading, or making the call you owe someone. Ask honestly whether meeting it would change anything. If the answer is no, do the smaller version of the thing today. Do not wait for the condition to arrive.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said they would only believe a messenger who brought an offering that fire came down and burned. The answer is simple. Messengers did bring that before, with clear proofs, and those people killed them anyway.

studies.title: You Are Not The First
studies.meaning: The shortest kind of consolation: not an explanation but a precedent. If you are being called a liar, so were the ones before you. The ayah then names what those earlier messengers carried, clear proofs, written pages, and a scripture that gives light, which raises the point rather than softening it. They were not denied for want of credentials. Commentators read the three items as one accumulation rather than three distinct books, listing the range of what had already been brought and refused.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing a stretch where demands and charges are quoted and answered one after another. The community had just taken losses at Uhud. In the city it was under steady attack in words. The early scholars report no special occasion for this ayah. They read it as the comfort that follows the argument before it, spoken straight to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).

keyTerms.note: Plural of a word for something inscribed, from a root meaning to write firmly or to build in courses. Translators render it as psalms, but it names the form a text takes rather than any single book.
An active participle: not lit, but lighting. The scripture is described as a source of illumination rather than something illuminated, and it is the same word the Quran uses of the moon.
A passive intensive form. The claim was not merely doubted; the man carrying it was accused. That is why the consolation offered concerns a person rather than an argument.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a society that kept its records in memory, calling a man a liar was the worst thing you could say about him. Contracts, debts and family lines all rested on what people testified. A man whose word failed once lost his standing in every later deal. The charge made in Mecca and Medina was aimed there: not at the claim, but at the man's use as a witness.
studies.didYouKnow: The three items listed here appear together in this order only twice in the Quran. Once is here. The other is at 35:25, where the sentence around them is almost a copy of this one. The two surahs are otherwise unlike each other in length and setting. The repeated sentence does the same comforting work in both.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah puts the problem in the hearers rather than in the evidence, and it does so by history rather than by assertion. It also says something about prophecy as a job. Being denied belongs to the work; it does not mean something has gone wrong. For a reader, that pulls apart two things people mix up all the time: whether a message is true, and how it was received.

crossReferences.why: Repeats this sentence almost word for word, with the same three items in the same order.
Adds what the earlier messengers did about being denied, which this ayah leaves unstated.
Makes the precedent explicit: even the accusations themselves are inherited from earlier arguments.

studies.applyIt: The next time you are misrepresented, resist the urge to correct the record straight away. Sit with it for a day. Notice how much of the sting comes from the accusation and how much from being unable to answer it. Then decide calmly whether answering would change anything for anyone other than you.
studies.explainEasier: If people call you a liar, that is nothing new. Messengers before you were called liars too. They came with clear proofs, with written pages, and with a book that gives light, and people still turned them down.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: The Enjoyment Of Delusion
studies.meaning: Three statements, each narrowing the last. Every soul tastes death. Wages are paid in full only on the Day of Resurrection. Success is defined by what is avoided: whoever is pulled clear of the Fire and let into the Garden has won. Nothing is said about degrees. The final clause does not call this life worthless. It calls it goods that mislead, which early scholars read as a comment on its scale rather than its reality.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This part of it answers people made bitter by loss, and by the taunts that followed Uhud. The ayah is general in form, and early scholars report no specific occasion for it. But its placement matters. It arrives among ayat about the dead, about wealth held back, and about mockery, and it answers all three with the same measure.

keyTerms.note: A participle, not a verb. Death is something the soul tastes rather than undergoes, which makes it an experience passed through and leaves the one tasting still there afterwards.
A doubled form suggesting repeated small tugs rather than one movement. The passive keeps the reader from being the agent, and the picture is of someone edged away from a place they were near.
Trade vocabulary for provisions or wares carried for a journey, useful and real but not the destination. The word is used elsewhere of a traveller's kit and of goods lent for a while.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan merchant carried two kinds of load: the trade goods he would sell, and the provisions he would eat on the way. The second kept him alive and was gone by the end. Nobody confused the water skins with the profit. Arabic used one word for both the wares and the travelling supplies, and this ayah puts the whole of worldly life in the second category.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence about every soul tasting death occurs three times in the Quran, at 3:185, 21:35 and 29:57. Each time it is followed by something different. Here it is recompense on the Day of Resurrection. In the second it is a test of good and bad. In the third it is a return to God.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Payment in full is put off, and that one move changes everything. If accounts are settled here, then every wrong left unpaid and every effort left unrewarded is a lasting injustice. If they are settled later, the present is a partial statement, not a final one. The passage also sets the bar for success very low and very firmly. Not rank, not honour. Simply being moved clear and let in.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the opening sentence and follows it with testing by good and bad alike.
Expands the closing image, comparing worldly life to vegetation that dries and crumbles.
Calls this life amusement and the final home the real life, in a Meccan surah.

studies.applyIt: Look at your calendar for the coming week and find the item you are most anxious about. Ask what will be left of it in ten years, and answer honestly rather than piously; some things will still matter. The ayah is not flattening the difference. It is asking you to actually make it.
studies.explainEasier: Everyone will die one day. You get what you earned on the day everyone is raised. Anyone kept away from the Fire and let into the Garden has won. This life can trick you.

studies.title: Tested And Spoken Against
studies.meaning: A forecast rather than a warning. Three things are named in advance: loss of property, loss of persons, and a steady flow of insult arriving from two directions. Saying it beforehand removes surprise, which is the whole purpose of the sentence. The response asked for comes as a pair, endurance together with mindfulness of God, and the closing phrase lifts it above mere coping. What is described is not survival but a course of action classed among the things that take resolve.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the years after the emigration. The community was poor, had just been beaten at Uhud, and lived beside groups that opposed it in speech long before anything else. Property left behind in Mecca was not coming back. The early scholars read the ayah as general preparation rather than an answer to one incident. They place it before the harder instructions of the later Medinan surahs.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to test by trial and also to wear something out through use. It carries two emphatic markers here, one at the front and one at the end, which is Arabic's strongest way of saying that something will certainly happen.

A word for injury that stops short of real damage: an insult, a nuisance, a wound to dignity. Naming it separately from loss of life and property keeps small persistent hostility from being dismissed as nothing.
The noun for a settled decision, the point at which wavering stops. The phrase it forms here classes certain courses of action as belonging to the kind of thing that requires that decision.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The emigrants reached Medina with almost nothing. Many took work carrying water or labouring in the date gardens of their hosts. Their houses in Mecca stood full of other people. Meanwhile mocking verse about them went round, made to be memorised and repeated. Insult was a public trade in Arabia with its own paid experts, and a family could be mocked in poetry for a generation.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase that closes this ayah names something as belonging to the matters that take resolve. It occurs three times in the Quran, and each time it describes patience. Here it follows persecution. At 31:17 it appears in a father's advice to his son. At 42:43 it describes forgiving someone after being wronged.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah treats advance notice as itself a kindness. Nothing about the trial is softened. What is removed is the second layer of suffering, the belief that hardship means something has gone wrong. It also places insult in the same list as death and material loss, refusing to rank suffering by how dramatic it looks. And it defines the required response as active rather than merely endured.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same forecast with a longer list, and adds the words the tested are told to say.
Ends with the identical phrase about resolve, attached there to patience over whatever befalls a person.
Instructs the Prophet on what to do with the abuse this ayah says will certainly come.

studies.applyIt: Count the criticisms you took this week that were about you personally rather than about your work. Then notice how much of your energy went towards them. Endurance here is not silence; it is refusing to let the smallest hostile voice set the agenda for your day. Choose one you will stop rehearsing in your head.
studies.explainEasier: You will be tested through your money and through your own lives. You will hear plenty of insults from people who were given scripture before you and from those who worship idols. Hold on and keep careful of God.

studies.title: Thrown Behind Their Backs
studies.meaning: A pledge is described as a duty to speak: make the scripture plain to people, and do not hide it. The passage then reports the failure twice, with two pictures. The first is bodily, putting a thing behind you where nobody can see it. The second is commercial, a sale at a bad price. The early scholars note that the pledge is about passing the scripture on, not about believing it. So what is condemned is holding back what was known, not being wrong about it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside a run of ayat spoken to those in the city who held earlier scripture. They were disputing the new message. The early scholars read the pledge as one taken from every group that was given a revelation. It is not a single event. Some tie the ayah to arguments about what earlier scripture held. They also record the view that the warning reaches anyone later trusted with knowledge.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to tie firmly. It is the strongest word for an agreement in the Quran, used of treaties and of the pledge taken from prophets, and it suggests a knot rather than a spoken promise.
The verb for tossing something aside carelessly, the way a date stone is discarded. It is not the word for refusing or for losing, which is what makes the phrase about their backs so pointed.
The price is not called wrong but small. That leaves the accusation a matter of judgement rather than of law, and the phrase recurs whenever the Quran describes something valuable being traded away.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Knowledge in seventh-century Arabia was carried by people, not on shelves. A man who could recite family lines or read out a contract held a place that depended on his being the only one who could. Scribes and scholars were consulted and paid, and their standing rose as what they held grew scarcer. Making everything plain to everybody would have cost them something real.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about selling for a small price comes up across the Quran. Each time, what is sold is a revelation or a pledge given to God, never an ordinary good. Two of those places are in this surah. One is here. The other is twelve ayat later at 3:199, where it describes people who refuse to make the sale.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes plain speaking a duty attached to knowledge, not a favour done to others. Receiving revelation is described as taking on a duty to people outside the circle that got it. So hiding it counts as a broken pledge, not just as holding back. It also implies that what they held cannot be turned into standing without loss. That is exactly what the picture of the price says.

crossReferences.why: States the same offence directly, naming concealment after clarification as the thing condemned.
Joins the same two elements, hiding scripture and selling it cheaply, inside a single sentence.
Describes people from the same communities who refuse this exchange, keeping the charge from becoming blanket.

studies.applyIt: If you know something that would help someone and have not said it, a name, a route through a process, a warning, send it today. Notice honestly whether some part of you enjoyed being the one who knew. That small pleasure is what the ayah describes, long before anything is actually sold.
studies.explainEasier: God took a promise from the people who were given the scripture. They were to make it clear to everyone and not hide it. They dropped that promise behind them and sold it for a small price. It was a bad trade.

studies.title: Praised For What They Did Not Do
studies.meaning: Two appetites are set side by side and treated as one condition. The first is being pleased with what a person has actually done. The second is wanting credit for what they have not. The sentence will not let the second count as a small vanity. It puts it under the same warning as the offences around it. The next ayah answers the question the first one raises, about who can grant or withhold praise, by naming the one to whom everything belongs.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources keep an exchange in which the ayah is explained two ways. One is about people who stayed back from a campaign, then came with excuses and expected thanks. The other is about people asked what their scripture contained, who held it back and let themselves be praised as though they had answered. The early scholars record both readings, and neither pushes the other out.

keyTerms.note: The verb for open delight. The Quran uses it approvingly elsewhere, so the fault named here is not the pleasure itself but where it has been attached, which the second clause supplies.
From a root meaning both to win and to be delivered. The same root gives the word for success used throughout the Quran, so escaping and triumphing are a single idea in Arabic.
Ownership with authority behind it, not bare possession. Placing it directly after a passage about reputation sets the whole economy of human praise inside something that does not depend on it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing in Arabia was built up in public and remembered aloud. A man's deeds were recited at gatherings, sometimes by relatives and sometimes by paid poets, and reputations outlived the people who earned them. There was no written record to check a claim against. A man who spoke well of his own share in a raid, in front of the right listeners, kept that credit for good.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for rejoicing used here is not condemned everywhere in the Quran. At 10:58 people are told to rejoice, in that case at God's grace and mercy. At 28:76 a wealthy man is told not to. The word carries no verdict of its own, and each passage is decided entirely by what the rejoicing has been attached to.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a failure that leaves no visible trace. Nothing was stolen and nothing checkable was said. A person simply accepted an impression they knew to be false. By putting that under a serious warning, the passage treats the inner accounting as the real one. The ayah that follows then removes the audience: if everything belongs to God, a reputation held on false terms is held nowhere at all.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same appetite operating inside a good deed rather than in place of one.
Names display as the fault in an act that is outwardly correct, the same inversion described here.
Gives a specific instance of wanting to be seen doing what one is not actually doing.

studies.applyIt: Recall a compliment you accepted this month that was slightly more than you had earned, where you let a wrong impression stand because correcting it felt awkward. You do not need to go back and fix it. Just name it to yourself accurately, once. The discomfort of doing that is the entire exercise.
studies.explainEasier: Some people are pleased with what they did, and they also love being praised for things they never did. They should not think they will get away with it. A painful punishment is waiting. Everything belongs to God anyway.

studies.title: Signs For Those Who Think
studies.meaning: The signs are said to be in two things: the making of the heavens and earth, and the turning of night into day. Sustained change is put alongside the structure itself. The second ayah describes who reads them, and it does so by posture rather than by learning. Remembrance in every position runs together with reflection, and the two produce a conclusion stated as a prayer, that none of this was made pointlessly.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. These lines close it, after long sections on Uhud and on debate with the People of the Scripture. The ayat step back from all of it to the plainest evidence available, which can be seen from anywhere. Classical commentaries keep reports of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) reciting these ayat when he rose at night. The passage is often read as the surah's summary rather than an aside.

keyTerms.note: From a root for succeeding and taking turns, the same root behind the word for a successor. It names night and day as replacements for one another, not merely as two different things.
The plural of the word for the kernel inside a shell, the edible part of a date stone or nut. Understanding is named as the pith of a person rather than an accessory to them.
A form of the verb implying effort applied to oneself and sustained over time. It is not a flash of insight but the deliberate turning over of something, and the grammar keeps it ongoing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Before clocks and street lighting, the sky was the instrument everyone used. Caravans crossed the desert at night by star. Herders read the season from where the sun rose on the ridge. Dates for debts and pilgrimages were set by the moon. Watching the sky was not contemplation for these listeners. It was navigation, timekeeping and weather forecasting, done by people who could not afford to be careless about it.
studies.didYouKnow: What begins here as observation turns into a prayer that runs for four ayat. It is one of the longer continuous prayers in the Quran. It ends with a plea not to be disgraced on the Day of Resurrection. The ayah right after it opens with God's response, answering the request directly rather than leaving it hanging.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Evidence for God is placed where anyone can reach it. That makes the argument open in a specific way: no text, no teacher, no language is needed first. The passage also joins two things usually kept apart. Remembrance is devotional and reflection is intellectual. Here the same people do both at once, in every posture. The conclusion they reach is about purpose, not about mechanism.

crossReferences.why: Lists the same signs at greater length, adding ships, rain and the movement of the winds.
Continues the prayer these thinkers speak, from the plea about the Fire to the final request.
Turns the same reflection inward, asking whether people have thought about themselves.

studies.applyIt: Go outside tonight for two minutes without your phone and look up. Do not try to feel anything. Just find one thing you can actually see, a single star or the edge of the moon, and stay with it long enough to be bored. The ayah describes people who did this often enough that it changed them.
studies.explainEasier: Look at the sky and the earth, and at how night turns into day. There are signs in that for people who think. They remember God standing, sitting and lying down, and say none of this was made for nothing.

studies.title: We Heard A Caller Calling
studies.meaning: The prayer moves from a fear to a claim and then to a request. Disgrace, not pain, is named first about the Fire, which tells you what these speakers dread most. Then they state their one credential, and it is deliberately small: they heard someone calling and they answered. Nothing about their merit is offered. Three requests follow, and two different words for wrongdoing are used in them, which the classical commentators discuss without settling whether the two are distinguished or joined for weight.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the closing passage of a surah that has argued, comforted and instructed for nearly two hundred ayat before it turns to prayer. The early scholars place the section late in the Medinan period. They treat it as a summing up rather than an answer to any incident. The speakers are the people described a few ayat earlier, thinking about the making of the heavens and the earth.

keyTerms.note: The verb for public humiliation rather than private pain. Naming this first says that what these speakers fear about the Fire is exposure, and the same root returns two ayat later as a request.
An indefinite noun: someone calling, not a named person. The vagueness is doing work, since the speakers describe their own moment of belief by the sound that reached them rather than by who made it.
