A plural from a root meaning breadth and dutifulness, especially towards parents. It names people whose goodness is expansive rather than merely correct, and the surah's closing ayat use it twice.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caller was a working office in that world. Someone with a strong voice climbed to high ground and called out news, an assembly, a lost camel, a summons to prayer. Everyone within earshot then had to decide what to do about a voice whose source they could not see. That daily experience is what this prayer uses to describe becoming a believer.
studies.didYouKnow: The prayer runs unbroken from 3:191 to 3:194. Every sentence in those four ayat is addressed to God, and the same words for our Lord are used five times. The classical collections report that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) would rise at night, look at the sky, and recite the closing ayat of this surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer shows a posture rather than a formula. It offers no achievements, only an answer to something heard, and then asks for what it has no claim to. Response first, request second, and merit never: that is the shape of prayer the Quran keeps returning to. It also treats forgiveness and good company as one thing. What is asked for at the end is not a place but people.

crossReferences.why: Closes another long surah with a prayer in the same voice, asking rather than claiming anything.
Opens this surah's prayers with the same address and the same anxiety about not lasting.
Ends another prayer with the identical request, to die in the company of the righteous.

studies.applyIt: Say these two lines tonight in your own words, and stop at the part where the speakers explain why they believe. They mention nothing they achieved. Try saying your own version of that sentence, naming the moment or the voice that reached you, without adding anything at all about how you have done since.
studies.explainEasier: Our Lord, anyone you put in the Fire has been shamed. We heard someone calling us to believe in you, and we believed. So forgive our sins, wipe away our bad deeds, and let us die among good people.

studies.title: The Promise You Never Break
studies.meaning: The last line of a long prayer asks for something already guaranteed. That is the interesting move. The speakers request what was promised through the messengers, which is not in doubt, and then supply the reason as a statement about God rather than about themselves. The only genuinely open request is the second one, to be spared disgrace. Commentators note that asking for a promised thing is a way of asking to be counted among the people it applies to.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, the final sentence of the supplication that closes this surah. The community it belongs to had just come through a defeat and was living inside the gap between what had been promised and what was visible. The commentators report no occasion for the ayah. They read it in place, as the natural close of a prayer that begins with reflection on creation and ends at the Day of Resurrection.

keyTerms.note: Not merely a promise but an arranged meeting, a place and a time agreed between two parties. The word turns the Day of Resurrection into an appointment that will be kept rather than an outcome that may arrive.

The same root used two ayat earlier of those admitted to the Fire. Repeating it turns that earlier statement into a request, so the prayer asks not to fall on the wrong side of a sentence it has just spoken.

The plural, not the singular. What is being claimed is not a promise made to this community alone but the accumulated promise carried by every messenger, which is why the request can be made with confidence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An appointment in Arabia was a serious thing because keeping one was expensive. Meeting someone at a named well on a named day meant crossing desert on the strength of a word, with no way to confirm anything on the journey. A man who failed to appear was remembered for it for years. The vocabulary of this ayah comes from that world of arranged meetings honoured at cost.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a fixed appointment occurs four times in the Quran, twice in this surah and twice elsewhere. Three of the four are statements made about God in the third person. This one is the only place where the sentence is turned around and addressed to God directly, inside a prayer: You do not break the appointment.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah rests a request on what God is like, not on the record of the person asking. That is a particular kind of confidence. It also does something unusual with promises. Treating God's promise as an appointment means two parties who both have to turn up. So the worry in the prayer is not whether God will keep the meeting. It is whether the speakers will be known when they get there.

crossReferences.why: Closes the surah's first prayer with the same guarantee, stated there about God rather than to Him.
Uses the same guarantee inside a passage about signs demanded and not supplied.
Asks for a promised thing in the same manner, here in a prayer made by the angels.

studies.applyIt: There is something you have been half-asking God for without saying it out loud, because it feels presumptuous. Say it tonight in plain words, then add the reason this ayah gives: not that you deserve it, but that He keeps appointments. Notice whether the second half changes how the first half feels in your mouth.
studies.explainEasier: Our Lord, give us what you promised us through your messengers. Do not shame us on the Day when everyone rises. We are asking because you always keep your word. You have never once broken a promise.

studies.title: You Are Of One Another
studies.meaning: The prayer is answered straight away, and the answer starts with a rule before it reaches any group. No worker's work is lost, and the ayah names both kinds of worker on purpose: male or female. A short clause says why the two cannot be held apart in the accounting. Each is from the other. Only then does the answer turn to a set of people who left home, were driven out, were hurt and fought. It promises them a covering over of their wrongs.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources report that a woman among the believers, Umm Salama, asked a question. The Quran spoke of emigration and reward in the masculine, yet women had emigrated and suffered too. This ayah came in reply. Several early collections carry the report. The hardships listed here, being driven out, being hurt and fighting, describe what the Medinan community had by then lived through.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb to answer that implies acting on a request rather than merely replying to it. The prayer of the four preceding ayat is met with a response that begins before any of it is restated.
The agent noun from the verb used throughout the Quran for deeds. Choosing the worker over the work makes the promise about persons: nobody who works goes unrecorded, whatever the work was.
From a root meaning to cover or conceal; the Quran uses the same root at 57:20 of sowers who bury seed under soil. Forgiveness is pictured as a covering rather than a denial that anything happened.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Emigration was not a journey but a taking apart. A household leaving Mecca sold nothing, since there was neither time nor a buyer. They walked out and left the house, the share in a well, the stored dates and the family graves. Women travelled in the same conditions as men, some alone. Some were held back by relatives who would not let them go.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah closes its list of hardships with two verbs built from a single root, one active and one passive: they fought, and they were killed. The classical reciters record more than one order for that pair, and the commentators discuss what each order implies. Nothing else in the list is doubled in this way.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The answer sets out that God's accounting does not run along the lines human societies use to rank people. The clause about being from one another is given as the reason, and it is a statement about origin rather than about entitlements. The ayah also does something careful with suffering. It does not explain it and does not call it good. It records it as work, and promises the work will not be lost.

crossReferences.why: States the same equality of reward for men and women, and adds a promise about this life.
Repeats the pairing in a legal setting, so the point is made twice in different registers.
Expands the pairing into a list of qualities named separately for men and for women.

studies.applyIt: Think of the work nobody sees you do: the early morning, the repeated cleaning, the phone call to a difficult relative. Name one piece of it today and let the ayah's own word stand for it. Not a small thing that goes unnoticed. Work, of the kind this passage says is never wasted.
studies.explainEasier: God answered them: I will not waste the work of anyone who works, man or woman. You come from each other. Those who left their homes, were hurt and fought will have their sins covered and gardens to live in.

studies.title: The Comfort That Runs Out
studies.meaning: An instruction about attention rather than about belief. What is warned against is being taken in by movement, the visible activity of people doing well, travelling for trade, coming and going with visible success. The passage does not deny the prosperity. It measures it: brief, and followed by something. Then the contrast is drawn without symmetry, since the second half runs longer and its verbs are verbs of staying. The early scholars gloss the word for their comings and goings as trade between markets.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, near the close of the surah. The Meccan opposition ran the caravan trade, and its wealth was on open display. The Muslim community in Medina was poor. The early scholars report that some believers looked at that contrast and were unsettled. These ayat answer the comparison rather than any argument. That is why they speak about being impressed rather than about being convinced.

keyTerms.note: From the verb to turn something over. Commentators gloss it as travelling for trade, coming and going between markets, so what is described is visible commercial success rather than political power.
The same word names the baggage a traveller carries and the pleasure a thing gives. Both senses assume a journey: it is what you use on the way, not what you arrive holding.
What a host sets before a guest on arrival, before the real hospitality begins. Applied to the Gardens it makes them the reception rather than the whole of what is finally given.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Meccan caravan year had a rhythm everyone in the Hijaz could watch. South towards Yemen in winter, north towards Syria in summer, hundreds of camels moving under armed guard. Wealth arrived in loads you could see, on animals you could count. For a poor household in Medina watching that traffic pass, the question of who was right could feel settled by what came down the road.
studies.didYouKnow: The two-word sentence calling it a brief enjoyment appears again, word for word, at 16:117. There too a mention of punishment follows straight away. Elsewhere the Quran makes the same measurement at much greater length. Here it takes two words, set between a warning and a promise that both run far longer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats envy as a problem of seeing rather than a moral failing. It corrects it by adding what was missing, which is how long the thing lasts. It does not say the wealth is unreal or unearned. What it denies is that a snapshot amounts to a verdict. That leaves room to admit somebody else's success honestly and still not want to trade places with them.

crossReferences.why: Uses almost the same sentence about not being deceived by their movement through the land.
Names the preference this passage corrects and gives two reasons, better and more lasting.
Applies the same word for brief enjoyment to everything given, not only to what opponents hold.

studies.applyIt: Pick one person whose life you have compared yourself to this month, probably on a screen. Instead of arguing yourself out of the feeling, add the missing information: what you actually know about their days, and what you do not. Envy usually runs on a very short clip. Lengthen it and most of its force goes.
studies.explainEasier: Do not be impressed by people who reject God moving about the land and doing well. It does not last long, and then their home is Hell. People who are careful of God get gardens with rivers, for good.

studies.title: Those Who Will Not Sell
studies.meaning: A qualification is placed near the end of a surah that has argued hard. After all that criticism, the passage says plainly that among the same communities are people who believe. They believe in this revelation and in what came to them, and they are lowered before God. The mark it gives is negative and exact: they do not sell God's signs for a small price. Their reward is held with their Lord, beyond the reach of the argument that has been running.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, the second to last ayah of the surah. The early scholars most often connect it to the death of a ruler abroad who had sheltered Muslim emigrants years earlier and had come to believe, when news of it reached Medina and prayers were said. Other reports read the ayah generally, of anyone from the earlier communities who accepted the message. Both readings are preserved side by side.

keyTerms.note: The word describes a body as much as an attitude: eyes down, voice quiet, movement stilled. The Quran uses the same word at 41:39 of land that has gone flat and silent before rain arrives.
The word for what is paid, not for what is bought. The idiom of selling revelation for a price recurs through this surah, and here it finally appears as something refused rather than something taken.
A term from bookkeeping. Calling God swift at it says the tally is not a slow procedure, which matters at the close of a surah that has been counting things carefully for two hundred ayat.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina was not a sealed city. Traders, travellers and refugees moved between it and Syria, Yemen and the far side of the Red Sea, and news about people travelled with them. A group of early Muslims had spent years abroad, under the protection of a foreign court. Communities were not the closed blocks later readers imagine. One family could hold several loyalties at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about selling God's signs for a small price occurs twice within a dozen ayat of each other in this surah. At 3:187 it is an accusation; here at 3:199 it is praise. The same measure is applied to two groups drawn from the same communities, and it returns opposite results.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah stops a long argument from hardening into a verdict on a whole people. It takes nothing back from what was said earlier. It simply moves from communities to persons, and offers a test that a given person either meets or does not. It also treats reward as held with God, not handed out by any community. That takes the question of who counts as an insider out of human hands.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same qualification earlier in this surah, in almost the same terms and at greater length.
Describes the recognition itself, which this ayah reports only as an accomplished fact.
Names people who believed on hearing it because of what they were already holding.

studies.applyIt: Think of a group you hold a settled opinion about, then name one actual person inside it whom you know. Notice how fast the general judgement stops applying. This ayah does exactly that at the end of a long argument. You can do it in one sentence, before you next repeat something about a group.
studies.explainEasier: Not everyone who was given scripture before turned away. Some of them believe in God, in what came to you, and in what came to them. They are humble, and they will not sell God's words cheaply.

studies.title: Endure, Outlast, Hold The Line
studies.meaning: Four commands in rising demand. The first is patience in your own difficulty. The second is a competitive form, meaning to outlast others in it. The third comes from a root for tethering horses at a frontier, and is read as holding position, staying bound to a post. Awareness of God follows. Then the outcome is left as a hope, not a guarantee, which early scholars note about the closing particle.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This is its final ayah. The surah has spent much of its length on a defeat, on grief, and on argument with neighbours who rejected the message. Nothing more of the story is left to tell, so it ends with instructions instead. Early scholars report no particular occasion, and read the closing address as gathering up everything the surah has just worked through.

keyTerms.note: The root carries restraint and confinement, used of penning an animal or holding a person in place. Patience here is closer to staying put under pressure than to accepting something calmly.
A reciprocal form of the same verb, implying patience exercised against someone else's, as in a contest of endurance. Early scholars read it as outlasting an opponent or as sustaining one another.
From the root for tying, and for the tether that binds a horse. Classical readings range from guarding a frontier to keeping oneself bound to prayer after prayer.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Horses were rare and expensive in Arabia. They were kept by few and prized above camels for speed. A man who tethered one at the edge of a settlement was committing a serious asset to waiting. He was feeding an animal that ate more than it earned, on the chance of a raid that might never come. The word chosen for the third command carries that picture of costly readiness.
studies.didYouKnow: Two of the four commands in this ayah come from a single root, placed in two different verbal forms one after the other. Arabic can do this without sounding repetitive because the second form turns the action outward towards someone else. English needs two unrelated words to carry the shift.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Endurance is given three shapes rather than one, and the movement is outward: alone, then against a rival, then at a post held for others. That refuses the idea of patience as private resignation. The closing verb is left open, so even after all four commands the result is stated as something hoped for. Nothing in the sentence lets obedience become a claim on God.

crossReferences.why: Pairs patience with prayer as the two things to seek help through, and promises God's company.
Ends its own short list with mutual counsel in patience, making endurance something exchanged.
Uses the same root for tethered horses, in the language of preparation and readiness.

studies.applyIt: Choose one thing you have been quitting again and again, and set a smaller version of it that you will keep for seven days. Not a better version, a smaller one. The ayah puts holding position alongside enduring. Holding position means being there tomorrow, which is a different skill from trying hard today.
studies.explainEasier: Be patient when things are hard. Keep going longer than the people who are testing you. Stay at your post. Keep God in mind, and you may do well.
